articles.title: New Hampshire Senate race tightens, Rhode Island governor on track to lose: 5 primaries to watch
articles.summary: New Hampshire and Rhode Island will serve up some of the last major primary contests of the 2026 election cycle, showcasing a likely upset in the Rhode Island governor’s race and bitter battles in the contest for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat. Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and scientist Karishma Manzur will face off for the…
articles.body:
New Hampshire and Rhode Island will serve up some of the last major primary contests of the 2026 election cycle, showcasing a likely upset in the Rhode Island governor’s race and bitter battles in the contest for retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen’s (D-N.H.) seat.

Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) and scientist Karishma Manzur will face off for the senator’s seat on the Democratic side — a primary that some polling suggests may be tightening. Meanwhile, former Sens. John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) and Scott Brown (R-Mass.) have mounted comeback bids in the race.

The Granite State’s Democratic primary for Pappas’s seat has turned into a war of words between front-runners Maura Sullivan and Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of Jeanne Shaheen, as the pair has traded barbs over nepotism and corporate influence.

Over in the Ocean State, incumbents are trying to fend off serious primary challengers in the Democratic contests for governor and Providence mayor as Democratic primary voters have made clear their largely antiestablishment and anti-incumbent mood.

Here are five primaries to watch in New Hampshire and Rhode Island:

New Hampshire Senate contest down to the wire

The Democratic contest for New Hampshire’s Senate seat is coming down to the wire on Tuesday as Pappas looks to fight off a challenge from Manzur and three other long-shot challengers to replace Shaheen.

Long viewed as the front-runner, Pappas has been endorsed by high-profile Democrats like Shaheen and former Vice President Kamala Harris, while Manzur has picked up endorsements from former Rep. Jamaal Bowman (D-N.Y.) and several Democratic state lawmakers.

Polling, too, has shown Pappas as the clear front-runner , though some has suggested the congressman’s lead over Manzur has narrowed.

Polling from the University of New Hampshire Survey Center released late last month showed Pappas leading Manzur by 13 points. Meanwhile, polling released by the Saint Anselm College Survey Center at the New Hampshire Institute of Politics just six days prior showed the congressman holding a 31-point lead.

There’s been increased scrutiny on the accuracy of polling after surveys overstated Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s expected win against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) and pollsters’ incorrect prediction that democratic socialist Francesca Hong would easily win the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary.

Manzur has contrasted herself with Pappas by arguing he’s been supported by — and therefore beholden to — special interest groups, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). Pappas’s campaign has argued that Manzur’s campaign has misconstrued how much Pappas has received from the pro-Israel lobbying group and has argued that he doesn’t take contributions from corporations’ political groups.

Pappas’s pitch to voters has been that he has a legislative track record of getting things done in Congress and points to the coalitions supporting his campaign, including organized labor and small businesses.

2 ex-GOP senators look to gain foothold back in Congress

Two former Republican senators are duking it out for the chance to return to their old day job in Washington, D.C., even as all signs point to an easy victory for one of them.

Sununu, who’s served in the House and Senate for a combined 12 years, threw his hat in the race after his brother, former New Hampshire Gov. Chris Sununu (R), declined to run for Shaheen’s seat.

Meanwhile, Brown, who represented Massachusetts in the Senate between 2010 and 2013 before later making two unsuccessful bids in both the Bay State and New Hampshire, is mounting a long-shot challenge.

John E. Sununu is backed by key members of Senate Republican leadership such as Sens. Tim Scott (S.C.), chair of the Senate Republicans’ campaign arm, and John Barrasso (Wyo.), the No. 2 Senate Republican. Polls have consistently shown him comfortably leading Brown by double digits.

Brown, who previously served as U.S. ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa under President Trump, has been endorsed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and New Hampshire House Speaker Sherman Packard.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates Shaheen’s seat as “lean Democrat.”

The Democratic primary to replace Pappas in New Hampshire’s eastern 1st Congressional District has turned ugly and personal between front-runner candidates Stefany Shaheen and Sullivan.

Shaheen, a healthcare business owner, has attacked Sullivan, who served as a top aide in the Veterans Affairs Department during the Obama administration, for her campaign donors.

She has accused Sullivan of taking donations from AIPAC, Palantir and others. AIPAC has become a focal point in the midterms amid the party’s divided opinion over how far to support Israel; Palantir donations have also become a source of tension in some primaries given it’s a contractor for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Meanwhile, Sullivan has hit back, launching an ad that describes the younger Shaheen as a “fancy last name” and accuses her of feeling “entitled to your vote.”

Seven other candidates are also running for Pappas’s seat on Tuesday. Some polling suggests that Sullivan holds a single-digit lead over Shaheen. Cook Political Report rates the open House seat as “likely Democrat.”

A bridge threatens to topple Rhode Island governor’s reelection

The 2023 closure — and slow reconstruction — of Rhode Island’s westbound Washington Bridge has emerged as a flash point in the state’s gubernatorial rematch between Gov. Dan McKee (D) and former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, as the incumbent has received pushback for his administration’s handling of the job.

The bridge was closed nearly three years ago after engineers identified structural issues that they feared could cause the bridge to ultimately collapse, prompting state officials to close a major transit route that connected Providence to East Providence.

McKee has drawn frustration and anger from residents over the state’s slow process to demolish and replace the westbound bridge; he notably did not attend the first press conference where news of the bridge closure was revealed.

Demolition of the bridge finished in December — the governor points out it happened ahead of schedule — and completion of the next bridge is expected by 2028.

“I know there is a lot of frustration, and I accept it,” McKee told The New York Times in a recent interview. “But in the end, people are going to realize we did the right thing.”

McKee and Foulkes faced off against each other in 2022, with the governor edging out his opponent by just shy of 3 points in the primary. McKee has attacked Foulkes over her tenure at CVS and its ties to the opioid crisis. CVS reached a settlement in 2022 to pay states $5 billion for its role in the epidemic.

On the campaign trail, Foulkes has acknowledged that CVS made mistakes but argued that the retailer was “the only chain that cut off over 600 pill mill doctors,” according to The Providence Journal .

“We had an almost 40 percent reduction in opioids under my watch. … What that meant is when someone came to the pharmacy with a prescription from one of these doctors based on the DEA [Drug Enforcement Administration] number, we had to send them away, but they could go down the street and fill it,” she told an attendee at a campaign event, according to the Rhode Island news outlet.

Public polling has shown Foulkes with a healthy lead over McKee. Whoever wins the primary on Tuesday will be the heavy favorite to win in November.

Democratic socialist looks for upset in Providence mayoral primary

Rhode Island could see another incumbent ousted this week as Providence Mayor Brett Smiley (D) looks to fend off a challenge from democratic socialist state Rep. David Morales.

Morales has been likened to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, another democratic socialist, given his social media-driven campaign and focus on affordability. He also enjoys the support of key progressives such as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

Meanwhile, the mayor has leaned on his track record while hitting Morales over previous remarks he made about law enforcement, and he suggested the state lawmaker isn’t introducing new ideas.

Smiley has been endorsed by former Rhode Island Gov. Gina Raimondo (D) — he served as her chief of staff — former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg (D) and Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha (D).

articles.title: Vulnerable Republicans divided over wisdom of Trump’s midterm convention
articles.summary: Republican senators and candidates have mixed feelings about President Trump’s midterm election convention, with many hoping that Trump can rev up millions of MAGA voters but worried of being tied to a president with a slumping approval rating. Party officials are promising a big turnout of Senate Republican incumbents at this week’s convention, which Trump…
articles.body:
Republican senators and candidates have mixed feelings about President Trump’s midterm election convention, with many hoping that Trump can rev up millions of MAGA voters but worried of being tied to a president with a slumping approval rating.

Party officials are promising a big turnout of Senate Republican incumbents at this week’s convention, which Trump allies will host Wednesday and Thursday in Dallas, but GOP strategists are warning Republican senators and candidates in tough races to stay away.

They say GOP candidates in tough races this fall face a risk in letting themselves get more closely tied to the president only weeks before the election.

“Trump is an absolute albatross for Republicans running in tight races because he promised to focus on the economy and keep us out of foreign wars and the exact opposite has happened,” said a senior Republican strategist who requested anonymity to talk about Trump’s impact on the election.

“By having a Republican candidate attend the convention, you’re tying yourself immediately to the president,” the strategist added.

“You’re already defending a voting record that you may have in the House or Senate if you’re an incumbent and then on top of it, you have to defend anything the president says at the convention, anything anyone else says at the convention, because if you’re there, you’re tied to it,” the source said. “It makes it a lot easier to avoid headaches and issues that your opposition can bring up if you simply [do] not attend and focus on your campaign on the ground.”

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), one of the Senate’s most vulnerable incumbents, has decided to stay away from the GOP gathering in Texas.

A spokesperson for Collins told the Portland Press Herald she “runs her own campaign independent of any national party schedule.”

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who may face a tougher-than-expected challenge in a Republican-leaning state, said his time is better spent meeting with constituents in South Dakota and that he won’t attend the convention.

“I’m back in the state of South Dakota,” Rounds said when asked about the convention.

“I do coffees. What I do is I go on out” and meet constituents, he added. “I think I’ve hit 14 different communities since I’ve been back.”

Asked if the midterm convention is a good idea, Rounds said, “That’s up to the folks that want to be there.”

“I’m not going to be there,” he added. “If I got time off, I try to spend it in South Dakota.”

Rounds’s independent challenger, Brian Bengs, released an Impact Research poll of 500 likely South Dakota voters last month showing him tied with Rounds, 44 percent to 44 percent.

While Rounds is widely seen as safe to win reelection, the poll underscores why Republicans aren’t taking any chances in a difficult election year for the GOP.

Trump’s trade war with Canada and his decision to allow the import of 300,000 metric tons of foreign-raised beef into the United States are unpopular with South Dakota voters.

Rounds said South Dakota ranchers viewed Trump’s decision to import hundreds of thousands of tons of foreign beef as a betrayal.

“The suggestion that they bring in 300,000 metric tons of beef is not a popular program. They feel just like the administration pulled the rug right out from underneath a lot of our farmers and ranchers,” he said.

Rounds said Trump is popular in South Dakota and folks “love the president” but “they’re hurt” and feel “let down” by the beef import decision.

A second GOP strategist who requested anonymity to talk about the midterm convention warned that Trump’s low approval numbers among independent voters is a “huge problem.”

“A lot of these close races will be decided by the independent vote,” the strategist said. “A lot of the more moderate Republicans are going to have to rely on the independent vote especially if Trump’s not on the ticket and not as many Republicans turn out.

“The independent vote is always important, but if it’s deteriorating, it’s not a good omen,” the source added.

Republican senators have agonized for months over polls showing independent voters shifting away from Trump and the GOP and toward Democrats.

A Civiqs tracking poll of registered voters across the country shows Trump is underwater with independents in key Senate battleground states such as Maine, Michigan, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska.

In Maine, for example, Trump has a 21-percent approval rating among independents and a 61-percent disapproval rating, according to the survey. In North Carolina, the president has a 28-percent approval rating among independents and a 65-percent disapproval rating.

In Ohio, the Civiqs survey found Trump with a 27-percent approval rating among independents and a 63-percent disapproval rating, while in Iowa it found Trump with a 24-percent approval rating among independents and a 66-percent disapproval rating.

Still, Republicans facing tough races this fall are hoping that Trump will drive GOP voter turnout and some plan to attend next week’s convention to help generate momentum and enthusiasm among base voters in their home states.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who faces a tougher-than-expected challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, the founder of the nation’s largest United Methodist Church, plans to attend the convention in Dallas.

“We’re taking nothing for granted,” said Marshall, who expects Democrats to pour tens of millions of dollars into the race to boost Hamilton.

The Kansas senator said, “We need the president’s base to get out and vote.”

“There may be 200,000 people in Kansas that only vote when President Trump is on the ballot,” he said. “Certainly he needs to communicate to them that he is on the ballot, that if we lose the House it will just be one impeachment after another — his agenda is over with.

“I think it’s real important that he’s able to communicate and get that base fired up,” he said.

Marshall said voters are feeling the sting of high prices, which has become one of the biggest issues of this election.

“This is one of the strongest economies I’ve ever seen, but at the same time people are still stinging from four years of Joe Biden’s inflation,” he said.

“We saw the cost of housing, healthcare, childcare, property insurance go up 50 percent in some four years,” he added, noting the consumer price index — a key inflation gauge — shows prices are rising by more than 3 percent a year.

Even so, Republicans got some encouraging news Friday when the Labor Department reported that employers added 162,000 jobs in August.

Other Republicans in tough races expected to attend the convention include Ohio Sen. Jon Husted and Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers.

articles.title: Ex-DSA member rips Abdul El-Sayed and warns far-left adopting politics of foreign terror org
articles.summary: A former Democratic Socialists of America member warns Marxists and Leninists have taken over the DSA and rips Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest.
articles.body: A former member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) who lives in Michigan issued a dire warning against extremism in American politics, and ripped far-left, progressive Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed as dishonest and "sanctimonious." "So, I think that it's up to everyone to not sit on their hands, Democrats, Republicans, Independents, we all need to be out there," Jake Altman told Fox News Digital. "We all need to be supporting candidates who love this country, who want to deliver for Michiganders. We should not be leaning into this sectarian politics. My fear is we've seen the left wing of the Democratic Party import the politics of Hezbollah into the United States, and now we're living with the sectarian aftermath of that." Altman, who formerly worked for several labor unions, said the DSA began adding fanatical far-left factions, including Marxists and Leninists, around 2014 and 2015. He claimed that at the time, similar far-left actors were taking control of labor unions, intending to use well-meaning workers as pawns in a much larger political battle to push the Democratic Party further left. That was about the time he left the movement, which he said has become "very susceptible to extremist takeover." FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT "That's not America," he said. "We want... a broad, tolerant America. We want pluralism here. We don't want to be at each other's throats. I'm just — we have to stand up and say 'no' to this." Tensions between the DSA and Democratic Party have reached a boiling point — nowhere more evident than in Michigan — where El-Sayed, who has palled around with socialist streamer Hasan Piker on the campaign trail, is facing difficulty rallying the party's moderates in support of his candidacy. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN "So, I've met Abdul several times," said Altman. "I worked very closely with his dad when his dad was union president of the AAUP local I worked for. So I have, you know, I think I have a pretty good read on the guy." Mohamed El-Sayed, Abdul's father, is an engineering professor at Eastern Michigan University, where he served as president of the school's AAUP chapter and led a faculty strike in 2022. "When I was at the Democratic Party convention, the recent Democratic Party nominating convention, [Abdul El-Sayed] recognized me," Altman continued, clarifying that he was referring to April's contentious Michigan Democratic Party endorsement convention. "He was working a line that I was standing in, and he recognized me, and he asked me, 'why all the hate?' 'cause I had been critical of the campaign up to that point." Altman said Abdul El-Sayed told him that his campaign "doesn't do that," apparently claiming that his campaign wasn't engaged in political mudslinging. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS "We see that the guy is not a straight shooter, he's not an honest broker," said Altman. "He, himself, said that his primary opponent, who I was supporting, couldn't string two coherent sentences together. I mean, the idea that he is somehow above it all is just not true. He's the most sanctimonious man in Democratic Party politics, and that's going a long way because there's a lot of sanctimony in that party." As for the DSA, according to Altman, it is unrecognizable compared to just a decade ago. "So, you had this older generation that was very tolerant, part of a broader liberal tradition, engaged in a productive way with the Democratic Party, not a destructive way as we see today," Altman explained. Part of that tradition, he said, was a total rejection of communism. But recently, the party voted to lift its ban on Leninists, allowing the proliferation of extremism among the party ranks. "We've seen in August 2025 that DSA at the convention voted to remove its prohibition on having Leninists operating within the organization," he said. "I mean, it doesn't get any clearer than this." He bemoaned current DSA co-Chair Megan Romer, whom he described as a "Marxist-Leninist" and "fan of the Cuban regime." HOW THE 'LONG MARCH' THROUGH THE INSTITUTIONS LED TO SOCIALIST TAKEOVER OF DEM PARTY: 'NEED TO WAKE UP' Romer traveled to Cuba last year with a group of 40 far-leftists, where she hyped the communist country as "care-focused vs. production-focused," blamed the United States' blockade for the country's food shortages and mass emigration, and said the country has "the most LGBTQ-friendly constitution in the world." Meanwhile, Abdul El-Sayed continues his attempts to try to win over moderate Democrats while also campaigning against Republican former congressman Mike Rogers ahead of the crucial 2026 midterms that will determine whether Democrats regain control of either or both chambers of Congress. Abdul El-Sayed has been dogged by questions about his affiliation with Piker, whom he invited on the campaign trail during primary season. He has refused to condemn Piker, choosing instead to brush him off as a "streamer from California" who has little connection with the Michigan race. articles.title: Netanyahu Was Personally Warned Hamas Was Planning ‘Terrifying Operation’ 10 Days Before Oct. 7 Attack: Report
articles.summary: The Emirati president reportedly warned Netanyahu that Hamas' leader told an intermediary in September 2023 that he was preparing "a terrifying operation."
articles.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan about Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar planning a major attack, but did not alert his security officials.

The warning about the impending attack was reportedly not passed on to Israel's top security officials, including former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi.

Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also separately contacted Netanyahu to warn about Hamas planning "something unusual," but Netanyahu insisted that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally and explicitly warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major attack roughly 10 days before the October 7 massacre , but dismissed the threat and did not alert his security chiefs, according to a shocking new Haaretz report.

The revelations come from research for an upcoming book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment , written by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval , who writes for Haaretz .

United Arab Emirates President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan raised the alarm directly with Netanyahu during a 45-minute conversation, three senior foreign sources familiar with the exchange told the Israeli newspaper, and reportedly warned that Sinwar was preparing a major operation.

Netanyahu reportedly responded that he believed Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank and assured the Emirati leader that Israel was prepared for any scenario.

The warning was apparently never passed to Israel's top security officials. Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi both told Haaretz they had not been informed about the conversation.

The report said the Emirati leader intervened after concerns grew in the UAE over intelligence originating with a Palestinian intermediary who had contacts with both Hamas and Israeli security officials.

Sinwar had reportedly warned through the intermediary in September 2023 that he was preparing a "zilzal," or earthquake, later describing what was coming as "the mother of all surprises" and "a terrifying operation."

That intelligence reached the Shin Bet on September 15, according to Haaretz . Bar subsequently briefed Netanyahu and reportedly warned during a security assessment two days later that Israel was "on a collision course," recommending either offensive action or strengthened defenses around Gaza and the West Bank.

Haaretz also reported that Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel separately contacted Netanyahu around the same period to warn that Hamas was planning "something unusual, a terrifying operation." The prime minister, however, insisted again that Israel was in control and reportedly mentioned neither call during an October 1 security discussion about Hamas and Gaza.

The Prime Minister's Office categorically denied the central allegation in a comment to The Jerusalem Post .

"An absolute lie! Prime Minister Netanyahu did not speak with the president of the United Arab Emirates during the period in question and did not receive any warning from him," it said.

Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett , however, backed the report Tuesday, telling Tel Aviv-based radio station 103FM he "knew for a fact the report is true."

"Mohammed bin Zayed of the Emirates warned Netanyahu that Sinwar was planning an operation. Abbas Kamel , the head of Egyptian General Intelligence, also warned Netanyahu days before the massacre that a major operation was being planned," Bennett said. "I don't want to talk about my relationship with anyone. I'm telling you that I know this fact is true."

articles.title: Unearthed interview exposes what Talarico thought about 'tough-on-crime' tactics
articles.summary: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico pushed restorative justice over suspension and expulsion, linking school discipline to criminal reform.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once framed disciplinary practices in schools as an outflow of the ideas behind criminal justice reforms he hoped lawmakers would implement in Texas. "I’m recently excited about the formation of a bipartisan criminal justice reform caucus in the Texas House with prominent Democrats and prominent Republicans who understand that we have to move away from a tough-on-crime approach to a smart-on-crime approach, and that, I think, filters down to our schools," Talarico said in a 2020 interview on school disciplinary practices and their effect on minorities. Talarico’s train of thought from criminal reform laws to changes in educational discipline demonstrates his underlying beliefs about moving away from punitive corrections. SOROS NETWORK REBUILDS PROGRESSIVE PROSECUTOR PUSH AFTER STRING OF ELECTION LOSSES Talarico fleshed out his view, detailing how the changes would affect the educational system. "[We are] starting in elementary school, where we really pursue restorative practices that are going to rehabilitate our students who are suffering from trauma, our students who are feeling unsafe in school and our students who harm a classroom community." Talarico was referring to "restorative justice," a view that links misbehavior to past personal and emotional experiences. In the words of Texas Appleseed, a group that promotes "social, economic and racial justice," restorative justice in education emphasizes the relational cost of conflict as a way to deter future bad behavior. "Restorative Justice, when applied to a school setting, focuses on how student behavior has harmed others and how to make amends. Schools use it to build community and strengthen student–school connections," the group wrote in a definition submitted to lawmakers. The approach is often mentioned as an alternative to "zero tolerance" policies that focus on punishments that deter discouraged conduct. To Talarico, its adoption could deemphasize other forms of punishments. "What that means is really allowing students to repair the harms that they’ve caused in a classroom community. It's a lot more rigorous and a lot more effective than just expelling a student or suspending a student or removing them from a classroom community," Talarico said. While in the Texas legislature in 2021, Talarico introduced a bill, HB 62, which would have sought to move schools away from in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension and removing kids to alternative educational programs. The bill stalled in committee and never became law. NORTH CAROLINA TEACHER'S KILLING REIGNITES SCRUTINY OF ROY COOPER'S CRIMINAL JUSTICE RECORD IN SENATE RACE In the wake of the Uvalde school shooting in 2022, Republican lawmakers pushed back against Talarico’s line of reasoning, arguing that, despite some calls for leniency, repercussions for problematic behavior are sometimes unavoidable. "Look, I don't want to see a kid go to jail for being caught with some pot. I don't want to see a kid go to jail because he gets into a fight with another kid," Texas state Rep. Steve Toth, a Republican, told interviewers. "That's clearly not the intent here. But if you've got a kid that is violent and is consistently violent, and they've been violent toward other children and teachers, then we either have to reach that kid or we have to remove that kid. They shouldn't be in the classroom. Period." Talarico’s statements are consistent with past calls to step away from law enforcement and prisons and towards social programs — calls that also show his beliefs about the best ways to deter criminal behavior. "If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing and spent it on education, health care, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete," Talarico said in a 2022 speech to a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students. A little later on in that same speech, Talarico went further, calling the idea of prisons themselves a kind of violence. "My experience as a teacher, a legislator, and a Christian tells me that birds don’t belong in cages; children don’t belong in cages; people don’t belong in cages. Poverty is violence. Pollution is violence. And yes, prison is violence," Talarico said. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS "I’m not asking you to join the system; I’m asking you to change the system. Dismantle this system of violence." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about his views on criminal justice and how they link to education, Talarico's campaign said he has always prioritized both safety and smart-on-crime approaches, noting that he had been a member of the state's criminal reform caucus. "James joined his Republican colleagues on this caucus because as a former public school teacher, James cares about keeping Texas students safe. James agrees with most Texans that we government should be smart-on-crime, and our students deserve all the support possible," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "While James has passed bills in the legislature to deny bail for violent criminals, crack down on violent felons and send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, Ken Paxton has abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected — allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe. Even Ken Paxton’s fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free," he added, referring to Talarico's Republican challenger, former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Having cleared the primary and secured his party's nomination, Talarico will face off against Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.

articles.title: Senate ‘pure toss-up’ ahead of midterms: DDHQ
articles.summary: Fight for control of the Senate hangs in the balance with just eight weeks to go until the midterm elections, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). The nonpartisan election analyst on Monday shifted its November forecast to “a pure toss-up” for the upper chamber of Congress for the first time since the beginning of June.…
articles.body:
Fight for control of the Senate hangs in the balance with just eight weeks to go until the midterm elections, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The nonpartisan election analyst on Monday shifted its November forecast to “a pure toss-up” for the upper chamber of Congress for the first time since the beginning of June. DDHQ said it based its rating on an average seat outcome across 1 million simulations.

The new forecast is a slight change from the end of August, which found Republicans with a 2-point average lead over Democrats in Senate races.

DDHQ predicts Democrats will retake control of the House in the November contests. The election forecaster pegs the likelihood of the outcome at 67 percent as of Tuesday.

Other election analysts and polls have also indicated it will be a tough battle between Democrats and Republicans for majority control of the Senate. The GOP currently has a 6-seat advantage in the chamber, with 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats.

The Cook Political Report rates six Senate races as a “toss up,” including five seats currently held by Republicans and the open Michigan race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.

The nonpartisan election forecaster also shifted the Texas Senate race to a “toss up” after four-term Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) lost his reelection bid in the GOP primary runoff race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton earlier this year.

Paxton is up against Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) in the November race. An Emerson College Poll from last month found the two candidates are neck and neck, with the Republican polling at 47 percent support and the Democrat at 46 percent.

Republicans are traveling to the state this week for a GOP midterm convention in Dallas to drum up excitement among the party’s voters. President Trump, Vice President Vance, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) are all expected to make an appearance at this two-day event.

Thune told South Dakota’s KELOLAND News last week that he is concerned about losing the majority in the upper chamber.

“I worry about that, for sure,” he told the local outlet. “I’m a realist, and I just think you, I don’t ever try and sugarcoat things. I think it’s a competitive environment right now. I think we got the highest-quality candidates.”

Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) has expressed confidence in his party’s chances of retaking the Senate this fall, saying last month that Democrats “now have multiple paths for the majority.”

“We found new states — Iowa, Texas — which people a year ago weren’t even paying attention to,” he said.

articles.title: Congress needs a plan to remove incapable lawmakers who refuse to step down
articles.summary: Democracy requires that voters choose the people who represent them. But it also requires that the people charged with that responsibility must be able to discharge it.
articles.body:
Aging is hard. It often brings illness and infirmity. Aging in the public eye is even harder. Just ask Mitch McConnell , Kay Granger or Dianne Feinstein.

And as the Bipartisan Policy Center notes , years ago, “Senator Karl Mundt of North Dakota suffered a stroke and was absent from the Senate for the final three years of his term. Illness forced Senator Carter Glass of Virginia to be absent from the Senate for nearly two years. In the case of Glass, citizens of Virginia petitioned courts to remove Glass from his seat, as it was effectively vacant. The court refused to take action.”

These are just a few of the names of members of Congress who have continued to serve long after they were equipped to do so. Each of them stayed on in spite of suffering debilitating illnesses, and there was nothing their colleagues could do other than expel them through a disciplinary procedure. That has never been done.

Congress needs to establish a separate procedure to address situations when members cannot discharge their duties. Because Congress determines the qualifications of its members and can remove them, there is no need for the equivalent of the 25th Amendment to the Constitution to deal with congressional inability to serve.

The average age of senators is now around 65 . Thirty senators are over 75, with Sen. Charles Grassley (R-Iowa) topping the list at 92. In the House of Representatives, which skews younger, there are 18 members over 80 .

But age in itself is not the issue. As Idaho’s 82-year-old Sen. Jim Risch told NBC, “You got to like the job, and you got to have enough time to spend with your family, and you got to have your health, and if you’ve got your health and you’re doing what you want to do, why not?”

Age is only relevant when it causes illness or infirmity that prevents someone from doing his or her job. The Constitution says nothing about either, although it does contain language about what should happen in the event of a vacancy caused by the death or resignation of a member of Congress.

Some have proposed using the constitutional amendment process to address congressional incapacity.

For example, in August 2023, Professor John Martin of the University of Virginia School of Law called for an amendment that would “permit members of Congress to temporarily transfer the duties of their office to an interim appointee in times of short-term incapacity … [and] create a process for involuntary transfers of such duties whenever a member of Congress has a long-term incapacitation but is unable or unwilling to use the voluntary transfer process or resign.”

He contends that such an amendment is necessary because the Constitution sets fixed terms for senators and representatives. But also, it also grants exclusive power to Congress when it comes to judging the qualifications of its own members, and courts are reluctant to interfere with its determinations.

Congress has broad discretion when it comes to deciding whether to expel a member; there is no reason why such discretion cannot be applied to removal for non-performance of duties. So, legislation or congressional rulemaking seems to me the right way to go.

On July 16, Reps. Seth Moulton (D-Mass.) and Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.) offered one version of what a legislative approach would look like. Their proposal would require members of Congress to disclose if they plan to be absent for 21 days or more. The required disclosure would have to be filed within five days of when members believe they will be absent, and it includes a provision requiring an “honest” statement of the reasons for the absence.

“Transparency isn’t optional in public office,” Moulton argues . “People deserve to hear directly from the member representing them about whether they’re able to carry out the duties of the job they were elected to do. The Duty of Transparency Act simply asks members to be upfront with the people who put them there.”

That is a good step, but more is needed.

Congress should also establish a procedure to investigate instances in which members go for extended periods without attending congressional sessions or casting votes. If it is determined that a member is incapacitated and unable to do what they were elected to do, then the chamber in which they sit should be able to remove them by a two-thirds vote, as is now required for expulsion.

This would not be, and should not be, an easy thing to do. But right now, some members think it is acceptable to remain in Congress long past the time when they should step down. Alas, that seems too easy for them to do.

Democracy requires that voters choose the people who represent them. But it also requires that the people charged with that responsibility must be able to discharge it.

Just as we fight to preserve the first principle, we should also defend the second one.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: US rebuilding weapons stockpile could delay orders from allies
articles.summary: Patriot missile stockpiles have dropped to 36% of pre-Iran war levels as allies face delayed deliveries and U.S. rebuilds its defense inventory.
articles.body: The U.S. has for years been the top weapons supplier in the world. Over the past five years, arms exports have gone to nearly 100 countries. "These weapons are sought after around the world because we have the best weapons," said War Department Under Secretary for Acquisition and Sustainment Michael Duffey. The Trump administration says some of the U.S. stockpile depletion is because of the weapons given to Ukraine. The Center for Strategic and International Studies assesses those transfers have been a minor factor in the shrinking U.S. inventories except for one important tool – the Patriot Missile Defense System. WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST "We've maxed out the production lines now, and that process began during the Ukraine War when it was clear that modern conflict was going to require a lot more munitions than we had been planning on," said Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marine colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department. Between 2021 and 2025, Ukraine was the largest recipient of major arms around the world, with at least 36 countries supplying weapons. The U.S. was the top supplier over the five-year time period, accounting for 41% of Ukrainian arms imports. AS CHINA TENSIONS LOOM, US TEMPORARILY PAUSES TAIWAN WEAPONS SALES DUE TO IRAN WAR, ACTING NAVY SECRETARY SAYS Before Russia’s war in Ukraine began in 2022, CSIS estimates the U.S. had around 2,200 Patriot missiles in its inventory. Estimates show around 600 missiles were given to Ukraine, with a few of those possibly coming from U.S. allies. Deliveries of new production outpaced the number given to Ukraine, with an estimated 2,300 missiles in the U.S. Patriot inventory before the Iran conflict began. It’s estimated that around 36% of Patriot Interceptors remain from the pre-Iran war inventory. "As chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, my job is to sign off on all foreign military weapons and sales to countries like Israel, to countries, like Taiwan and Ukraine, for that matter. And when we can't deliver on that promise because we can't make those weapons fast enough, it hurts our alliances, it hurts allies' ability to protect themselves," said Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas. Publicly available government reports show at least four countries, including the U.S., have provided full Patriot missile systems to Ukraine. The U.S. is the only country that manufactures the Patriot battery, and one of two countries, along with Japan, to publicly show it produces Patriot missiles. "If we take all of the Patriots for ourselves, and of course, that's 600 a year, we can refill the inventory much more quickly, but we have frozen out our allies and partners," Cancian said. UKRAINE SEEKS MORE US PATRIOT INTERCEPTORS AS BOMB SHELTER PROBE DEEPENS Patriot producer Raytheon says, "Patriot is the foundation of integrated air and missile defense for 19 nations." But as the U.S. prioritizes rebuilding its weapons inventory, deliveries for some countries are already delayed. "Unfortunately, the world we live in is an increasing threat, and that means that we need a bigger military force, and we need a stronger defense industrial base to be able to equip the warfighter and supply all that we need to win the fight," Duffey said. Patriot batteries and Tomahawk missiles were first used in Operation Desert Storm. At least two other countries have Tomahawks and while the stockpile remains large compared to other systems, at around two-thirds of its prewar inventory, new orders from Japan and the Netherlands could face delays. "With Tomahawk, we have the same situation with the Japanese. They bought 400. They're told they're being pushed back in the queue. On the other hand, they're facing China. They've reconfigured one of their ships to take the Tomahawks. So, there's again going to be a diplomatic discussion there," Cancian said. MORE THAN HALF OF SOME US WEAPONS STOCKPILES USED IN IRAN WAR, RAISING CONCERNS ABOUT CHINA THREAT Just the U.S., the UAE and Saudi Arabia have THAAD systems. Their first confirmed use was in 2022 after a UAE system intercepted missiles launched by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. No official delays have been reported for THAAD orders, but the U.S. has 52%-62% of its inventory remaining and outstanding deliveries for Saudi Arabia, expected to be completed by April 2028. "This military competition we're in with China and Russia and Iran is real. And we have to win that competition," McCaul said. OPINION: AMERICA FACES A CRISIS IN OUR MILITARY ARSENAL THAT TRUMP IS RACING TO FIX The ground-launched Precision Strike Missile (PrSm), developed by Lockheed Martin, was first used in Operation Epic Fury. CSIS says just 10-22% of those weapons remain from pre-Iran conflict levels, following the ceasefire expenditures and revised estimates from the beginning of the conflict in late February. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's important to keep in mind that the level of intensity in those 14 days of renewed conflict were not as high as they were during the first 39 days of the air war," Cancian said about the July strikes after the ceasefire ended. "During the 14 days, the U.S. was launching maybe 80 to 100 strikes according to the Pentagon per day. During the 39 days of the major air war, we were launching about 350 strikes a day, plus Israel was launching another 200 to 250. articles.title: Office mandates are not a loyalty test
articles.summary: Remote work stopped being a pandemic exception. Leaders who keep asking whether they can force people back will keep fighting yesterday’s argument.
articles.body:
Remote work just received a fresh analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, and it should reset the return-to-office debate.

The new study of Census Bureau Current Population Survey data found that nearly 22 percent of U.S. workers ages 16 and older worked from home at least some of the time in 2025, down less than 1 percentage point from 2024. Hybrid work increased slightly while fully remote work shrank slightly; average remote hours slipped only from 27 to 26 hours over the measured period. This suggests a plateau in remote work where many executives expected a retreat.

What’s more, the remote work plateau has persisted even as return-to-office announcements multiplied.

The study also found a reshuffling across industries, with public administration remote work dropping 6 percentage points from 2024 to 2025 and information-sector remote work dropping about 5 percentage points. That pattern points to a correction, rather than a broad workplace reset. The distinction matters because leaders often confuse policy announcements with operating reality.

The Minneapolis Fed noted that professional services, finance, health care and social assistance hold high concentrations of remote workers, partly because those sectors contain more remote-capable work. Kastle’s office-entry data adds another check on the story: Its 10-city barometer reported a 55 percent weekly office occupancy average in June 2026 , with Tuesday the peak day at 65 percent.

That should move the executive question away from symbolic control. A blunt return-to-office mandate may satisfy a leader’s frustration, but frustration makes for a weak management system. Pew Research found that 75 percent of remote-capable employed adults work remotely at least some of the time. Among workers who currently work from home at least sometimes, 46 percent said they would be unlikely to stay if their employer removed that option. Labor-market power may shift, but preference does not vanish.

The worker preference also has nuance. Pew found that 72 percent of hybrid workers would choose a hybrid arrangement rather than a schedule that is full-time home or full-time office. Employees are choosing control, not disappearance. They want autonomy over where work happens when the task allows it. They also want connection, mentoring, sponsorship and social context when the office creates real value. The managerial challenge involves designing that trade-off explicitly, instead of hiding behind uniform attendance rules.

The strongest evidence supports structured flexibility. A randomized trial published in “Nature” found that a two-days-at-home hybrid schedule reduced quit rates by one-third among 1,612 employees at Trip.com. The same trial found no evidence of damaged performance reviews or promotion rates over the follow-up period. That finding should matter to executives, because it addresses the central fear behind many office mandates: that flexibility will quietly erode performance. The better conclusion says structure beats both office nostalgia and a remote free-for-all.

The contrarian point deserves space. Remote work can weaken organizations when leaders fail to manage connection, feedback, career development and coordination. In addition, recent coverage of a “Science” study reported that remote work can increase isolation and mental-health strain , especially for people who live alone.

That risk strengthens the case for thoughtful hybrid design. It weakens both extremes: five days in the office for everyone and permanent isolation for people whose roles require learning, trust-building or dense collaboration. That creates a caution rather than a universal formula, while still showing why serious companies should test work arrangements against outcomes instead of copying whatever schedule dominates LinkedIn arguments that month.

Leadership demographics may push this debate in a more flexible direction over time. Researchers at the National Bureau of Economic Research found that younger firms and younger CEOs allow more work from home , with firms founded after 2015 permitting almost twice as much work from home as firms founded before 1990. They also found that CEOs under 30 allow 1.4 work-from-home days per week , compared with 1.1 days for CEOs age 60 or older. The finding shows that work-location policy reflects managerial assumptions, organizational age and leadership culture as much as productivity data.

Executives should treat the Minneapolis Fed’s new analysis as a warning against lazy certainty. It says work from home has become sticky enough that leaders need better tools than mandates. Those tools include role-based policies, team-level norms, purposeful office days, better onboarding rituals, clearer promotion criteria, and performance measures that separate visible activity from valuable output.

The next stage of flexible work will reward companies that make office time earn its place. Use the office for trust, mentoring, conflict repair, creative disagreement and shared identity. Protect remote time for writing, analysis, coding, focused client work and deep execution. A serious hybrid work strategy treats location as a design choice, not a loyalty test.

Remote work has stopped being a pandemic exception. Leaders who keep asking whether they can force people back will keep fighting yesterday’s fight. Leaders who ask when the office improves performance, when home improves focus and how managers can make both accountable will build the operating model the labor market has already chosen.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators . “

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: What’s in an economy?
articles.summary: Trump's economy approval sits at -33 points, but Democrats' competing visions on cost of living and inflation haven't won voters over either.
articles.body: Eight weeks from today, millions of Americans will choose their next congressperson. Poll after poll tells us that the state of the economy will shape their choice: it’s the top issue for voters by a wide margin and most Americans are in a sour mood about it. That’s not the end of the story. We’ve learned from previous elections that voters consider a wide range of issues when they vote. The "economy" has different meanings to voters. Optimism doesn’t win over voters on pocketbook issues. And this year, while voters aren’t happy with President Donald Trump’s economy, that hasn't yet made them enthusiastic about the Democratic alternative. These are the four rules to think about as we inch closer to the midterms. Meantime, Democrats inch closer to victory as the Power Rankings takes a fresh look at congressional races in Missouri and Ohio. 1. The economy is central to elections, but watch for related issues The importance of the economy to elections has been a golden rule since the early '90s, when Democratic strategist James Carville famously cited "the economy, stupid" as the most important focus for a campaign. Did you know it was only one of three orders he gave to candidates that cycle? The economy has been a top-three issue throughout the Trump era, including the last two midterm elections, where it was the most important issue for 47% of voters (2022) and 18% of voters (2018). If that 2018 figure feels low, it’s because healthcare (26%) and immigration (23%) finished ahead. That year, Republicans lost 42 seats. No wonder another of Carville’s three rules for candidates was "don’t forget health care." (The third was "change vs more of the same.") HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY' The state of the economy bleeds into other major concerns, including healthcare. But even a strong economy wasn’t enough to get the GOP out of that election unscathed. And healthcare looms as another important issue this year: it’s ranked close behind the economy in most surveys this year. 2. The economy means different things to voters When pollsters ask about voters’ views on the economy, they usually ask how important "the economy" or "the state of the economy" is, or whether they’re satisfied with Trump’s performance on that issue. In some important ways, Trump has a strong economic record. Just last week, the U.S. added 162,000 jobs, about triple what economists had expected. The unemployment rate was steady at 4.1%. The stock market also continues to grow, even as Iran and tariffs drive volatility. These have helped keep Trump’s overall economic approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s in multiple polls this summer. When pollsters ask only about Americans’ personal economic situation, things look tougher. TRUMP'S APPROVAL RATING PLUMMETS TO NEW LOW AHEAD OF CRITICAL MIDTERMS: 'MORE WORK TO DO' In a Reuters/Ipsos poll released last week, 32% of voters said they approved of Trump on the economy. But only a quarter approved of his performance on cost of living and 24% approved of him on inflation and prices. The costs of gas, food and other basic goods are the major factors driving this discrepancy. If Democrats deliver a strong result in November, it will come down to a presidential approval rating in the mid-20s on these issues. 3. Voters see through economic optimism In 2022, President Joe Biden faced similar headwinds: the economy was rebounding, especially if you looked at unemployment, but inflation hovered around the 8% mark all year. Gas prices came in around $3.75. The Biden administration kept selling the positives. First, inflation was "transitory." Then the president argued that "zero percent inflation" from one month to another was a win, despite the high annualized rate. Senior officials took victory laps on the unemployment rate. Voters rejected this messaging at the ballot box, delivering the House to the GOP after a net loss of nine Democratic seats and handing Biden a net approval rating of -23 points on the economy. Today, headline inflation is less than half that at 3.4%, while gas prices are a little higher at $4.15. Trump’s net approval on the economy currently sits at -33 points. The Trump administration is running a familiar playbook. Vice President JD Vance said last week that gas prices could be worse if not for the Trump administration. As Fox’s Gillian Turner noted on "Special Report," there are similarities between a comment like that and the statements Biden officials made four years earlier. These optimistic visions are likely to remain a tough sell to voters. 4. Economic dissatisfaction doesn’t make voters any happier about the alternative It’s easy to look at all this and think the Democrats are in for a big night in November. That’s certainly a possibility. But polls keep showing that voters are just as discouraged by the left’s economic messaging. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS Right now, Democrats are offering voters competing economic visions. Some, like Abdul El-Sayed and Troy Jackson, want a revolution that starts with "Medicare-for-all" and higher taxes on the wealthy. Others say they want to undo Trump’s agenda while keeping the core of America’s economic system in place. It’s not yet clear whether these visions are unappealing to voters or whether the contrast between them is the problem. Either way, in the Reuters/Ipsos survey, 36% of voters say Republicans are the better party to handle the economy, while 37% prefer the Democrats. The poll has a ±3.3pt margin of error. That’s not encouraging for Team Blue. If the Republicans hold relatively steady in November – also a possibility in this forecast – those results will explain why. House: Democrats remain in the lead as two seats fall away from the GOP Democrats are still the favorites to take the House this November, with 212 seats in their columns to the GOP’s 206. There are 17 seats that are so close they could go either way. Those seats tend to swing in one direction as votes get counted. On a good night for Democrats, that means 229 seats, while a good night for the GOP would still see them hold onto their current House majority. (A "great" night for either party would mean winning some of the seats that lean toward the opponent in this forecast. The Power Rankings puts seats in the "lean" category when they’re highly competitive, but one party has an edge.) The changes in this forecast, which see two seats fall out of the GOP’s columns, all come from Missouri and Ohio. Missouri: redistricting ruling flips one seat back to the Democrats and keeps another in contention Republicans picked up redistricting wins across the southeast after the Supreme Court’s ruling narrowing the scope of the Voting Rights Act this year. That includes Missouri, where Republican lawmakers redrew the Kansas City-based 5th District, currently held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver, who won re-election there by 24 points, to include more White, rural areas. That put the district into the Solid R column in the initial Power Rankings this year. Last Thursday, the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously blocked the new districts from being used unless voters approve them in a referendum. The order restores the state’s existing map, flipping Cleaver’s district back to Solid D. MISSOURI AG FILES PETITION ASKING SUPREME COURT TO REVIVE TRUMP-BACKED REDISTRICTING MAP (It also makes Missouri’s 2nd District more competitive. The rankings already had that district at Likely R; we’re keeping it there for now.) Missouri has appealed the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which could rule on the state ruling quickly. For now, Cleaver holds on to the 5th District. Ohio: Sherrod and scandal make the state more competitive Three races in Ohio are heading leftward. First, Ohio’s 7th District, held by Republican Max Miller. The congressman’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, has accused Miller of physically abusing both her and their young daughter. Miller denies the allegations and has suggested Moreno has mental health issues. Moreno is the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno, who Miller says is trying to take down his political career. The 7th District was already close for the ‘likely’ column, and after these headlines and some prodding from Republicans to drop out, it’s become highly competitive. It moves from Likely R to Toss Up. Meanwhile, in the southwest of the state, watch the 10th and 15th Districts, held by Republicans Mike Turner and Mike Carey, respectively. These shouldn’t be part of the Democratic playbook in a regular election year: they’re predominantly White and middle-class. Turner’s 10th District contains Dayton and some suburban areas; Carey’s 15th includes some suburban and exurban parts around Columbus and stretches to the rural south. As the Fox News Poll has shown twice now, Democrat Sherrod Brown is running a strong race for Senate; up eight points at 53% in May and August. That kind of performance could create a closer race than Republicans would like. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The "Mikes" have the clear advantage, but victory isn’t a sure thing. The 10th and 15th Districts move from Solid R to Likely R.

articles.title: Congress spends $7 trillion. Here’s how that math works out if you think of just $100
articles.summary: A breakdown of how Washington spends every $100 shows Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid and debt interest consume most of federal spending.
articles.body: You work. You get paid. Washington takes its cut. But have you ever stopped to ask one simple question: Where does the money actually go? Forget trillion-dollar numbers for a minute. Most Americans can't comprehend the difference between $1 trillion and $7 trillion anyway. Let's shrink Washington down to something we all understand: a $100 bill. In fiscal year 2025, the federal government spent roughly $7 trillion. Social Security alone consumed about $1.6 trillion. Major federal health programs, including Medicare and Medicaid, were another enormous piece. Defense approached $900 billion. WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER And then there's the number that should make every taxpayer spit out their morning coffee: interest. The federal government spent about $970 billion just on net interest on the national debt. Not roads. Not teachers. Not soldiers. Not Social Security checks. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS HAVE LOTS OF IDEAS, BUT HOW ARE WE SUPPOSED TO PAY FOR THEM? Interest. That means roughly $14 out of every $100 Washington spent went toward interest on money we've already borrowed. ‘THE ODYSSEY’ REMINDS US OF THE NIGHTMARE WE ARE LEAVING FOR AMERICAN CHILDREN Think about your own household budget. Imagine earning $100 and immediately throwing $14 in the fireplace because of credit-card balances you accumulated years ago. You'd probably say you have a spending problem. Washington calls it a budget. JOHN ADAMS MADE A TERRIFYING PREDICTION. AMERICA IS CLOSE TO PROVING HIM CORRECT So where did the rest go? Roughly speaking, out of every $100 the federal government spent in 2025, about $23 went to Social Security, approximately $26 went toward major health programs, around $13 went toward national defense, and about $14 serviced the interest on our debt. The remaining dollars funded everything from veterans' benefits and income-security programs to transportation, education, federal agencies and thousands of other government programs. You can argue all day about which of those programs are worthwhile. But here's the part Washington doesn't put on your receipt. We didn't have the $100. BILLIONAIRE BEZOS SUGGESTS NO TAXES FOR HALF THE NATION. IS THAT CRAZY OR OVERDUE? Federal revenues were only about $5.2 trillion while spending approached $7 trillion. The result was another roughly $1.8 trillion deficit in fiscal 2025. In other words, for every $100 Washington spent, it collected only about $74 and borrowed roughly $26 to make up the difference. Try that financial plan at your house. Earn $74. Spend $100. Put the other $26 on the credit card. Then do it again next year. And the year after that. SIX DIFFERENT WAYS THAT PROVE THE WEALTHY PAY A LOT MORE THAN THEIR ‘FAIR SHARE’ Eventually, your banker is going to have a conversation with you that nobody in Congress seems interested in having. This isn't a Republican problem or a Democratic problem. It's an American math problem. WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD Politicians love telling you about the benefits they're going to protect, the programs they're going to create and the taxes somebody else is supposedly going to pay. Nobody likes telling you the truth. We have promised ourselves a government we aren't currently willing to pay for. And taxpayers should demand something that every restaurant, grocery store and hardware store already gives us. Think about your own household budget. Imagine earning $100 and immediately throwing $14 in the fireplace because of credit-card balances you accumulated years ago. You'd probably say you have a spending problem. Washington calls it a budget. A receipt. Every year, Americans should be able to see exactly how Washington spent every $100 it collected and how much additional money it borrowed in our name. Because here's the number that scares me most. The Congressional Budget Office says net interest costs are projected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026 and could reach about $2.1 trillion annually by 2036 under current law. That's not a rounding error. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION That's money future taxpayers will send to Washington before Congress buys them a single bridge, missile or Medicare benefit. Americans argue constantly about whether our taxes are too high or too low. Maybe we're asking the wrong question. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Before Washington asks Americans for another dollar, taxpayers should be asking: What did you do with the last $100? CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM TED JENKIN

articles.title: Mamdani to release documents on 9/11 health impacts before 25th anniversary
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the release of more than 170,000 pages of records detailing air quality around Ground Zero in the months after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday that his administration will release more than 170,000 pages of documents shedding new light on the air quality around Ground Zero in the months following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. In a press conference at the City Hall Rotunda, Mamdani said these documents would only be the first release of information that will reveal new details about "what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it and how they acted to limit liability." Over the next year, hundreds of thousands of more documents will be released onto a public portal that will be freely accessible to every New Yorker, Mamdani said. The creation of the portal came about after the city settled a lawsuit from 9/11 Health Watch, an advocacy organization that sued to obtain the documents now being released. 9/11 FAMILIES URGE TRUMP TO DECLASSIFY RECORDS ON SAUDI ARABIA'S ALLEGED ROLE The first tranche of documents being released Tuesday on the portal will involve the 68 boxes of Department of Environmental Protection files that were found "a few years ago," Mamdani said. Also included in the release will be the Harding memo, a letter that was sent to Bob Harding, a deputy mayor under Rudy Giuliani. It was sent to him after the attacks on the World Trade Center, and it outlined that there could be tens of thousands of legal claims filed against the city. Jon Stewart, who has spent years advocating for 9/11 first responders, said at the press conference that the memo showed the city buried the truth about the toxic nature of the air for nearly 25 years. "There was poison in the air and on the ground and in the window sills and in your air conditioners and covering your pets and your clothes. And it stayed there for months," Stewart said. TRUMP'S 9/11 TRIBUTE TO FEATURE MASSIVE PIECE OF GROUND ZERO HISTORY AT WHITE HOUSE "Everyone knew. And now it's very clear that the city knew as well. And rather than take the steps to ameliorate the damage that that would cause to its citizens and to the people that were down there, they instead covered it up to get back to business as usual," Stewart added. The document release comes days before the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. The majority of people died at the World Trade Center after two planes were flown into the Twin Towers by al-Qaeda terrorists. In addition to the World Trade Center, hijackers struck the Pentagon, and a fourth plane crashed in rural Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to retake control of the aircraft. Officials repeatedly noted that 25 years later, more people have died from illnesses linked to the attacks than were killed on Sept. 11 itself. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The documents, officials said, show that asbestos remained present in parts of Lower Manhattan for months after the attacks and that benzene levels continued to spike near Ground Zero. "Now, we in the public know that City Hall, led by former Mayor Giuliani, predicted that thousands of responders and community members would face devastating long-term health consequences from these toxins," U.S. Rep. Jerry Nadler, D-N.Y. said at the Tuesday press conference. The next release of documents that will be released to the portal will concern correspondence in Mayor Rudy Giulani's office, who was leading the city at the time of the attacks, according to Steven Banks, the city's top lawyer. Banks said a third tranche will involve documents related to 7 World Trade Center, a skyscraper that was destroyed along with the Twin Towers and was subsequently rebuilt.

articles.title: House vote condemning socialism reveals problems for Democrats
articles.summary: The vote comes as democratic socialist candidates are winning primaries in heavily Democratic districts and are likely to enter Congress in January.
articles.body:
If Republicans wanted to set a political trap for Democrats by forcing a vote on a bill condemning socialism, they dropped the ball. Last Tuesday, the Republican-controlled House voted to approve a resolution condemning socialism, with eight Democrats crossing the aisle to back the measure.

Those eight Democratic Representatives — Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas), Henry Cuellar (D-Texas), Darren Soto (D-Fla.), Jared Golden (D-Maine), Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.), Don Davis (D-N.C.) and Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) — should be commended.

Although purely symbolic, the vote could have provided an important bipartisan rejection of socialism and socialist policies that are at odds with the U.S.’s longstanding commitment to capitalism, individual liberty and democratic institutions. The vote comes as democratic socialist candidates are winning primaries in heavily Democratic districts and are likely to enter Congress in January.

But while forcing politically charged votes before an election is nothing new, Republicans turned what could have been a meaningful statement into an overtly partisan maneuver. Attached to the resolution — which “condemns and denounces socialism in all its forms, including the Democratic Socialists of America and opposes the implementation of socialist policies in the United States” — was unrelated language calling to enact the SAVE America Act .

That act, which President Trump has repeatedly tried to force through the Senate even though Republican senators say the votes are not there, is widely opposed by Democrats. The inclusion of the SAVE Act language alienated Democrats who may otherwise have supported a clean resolution, squandering an opportunity for a more bipartisan rebuke of socialism.

A group of moderate Democrats — including Reps. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), Hillary Scholten (D-Mich.), Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.) and Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) — attempted to introduce an amendment condemning socialism without the voting provision, hinting they might have joined the eight Democrats who ultimately supported the resolution.

In fact, proof of the potential for a larger, more bipartisan rebuke of socialism came just days later. On Thursday, the House passed the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act , sponsored by Gottheimer and Republican Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.), with 33 Democrats voting in favor.

The bill would force colleges receiving federal student aid funding not to participate in boycotts of Israel, a clear rejection of the Democratic Socialists of America organization’s anti-Israel and pro-boycott, divest and sanction positions.

Prior to the socialism vote, Gottheimer issued a statement arguing that the inclusion of the SAVE Act showed Republicans were “not actually interested in getting people on record on whether socialists are part of the Democratic Party.”

He’s right. If Republicans genuinely wanted to establish whether Democrats would reject socialism, they should have offered a clean resolution. Instead, they gave Democrats an out. However, Republicans’ partisan maneuver should not allow Democrats to avoid the larger question this episode raised: What does the Democratic Party stand for?

The Democratic Party has largely built its 2026 strategy around opposition to President Trump and the congressional Republicans enabling his unpopular policies. Given Trump’s 40 percent overall approval rating , and an even lower 35 percent approval on the economy, this approach could be sufficient to produce substantial gains this November.

But telling voters they should vote against Trump is not the same as giving them a reason to vote for Democrats. Democrats already have strong positions on healthcare, reproductive rights, defending democratic institutions and expanding economic opportunity. But the party has not built those commitments into a broad, coherent agenda focused on voters’ top concerns: affordability, the economy, immigration, healthcare, and public safety.

This absence is likely a key reason the party’s favorability rating is 14 points underwater even while Trump and Republicans have serious vulnerabilities. It also has created an opening for the Democratic Socialists of America to fill the vacuum. If voters come to think the Democrats’ agenda is that of the socialists, Democrats will struggle to build the coalition needed to govern nationally.

Democrats could still take back the House — and perhaps the Senate — in 2026 due to dissatisfaction with Trump. But when the presidency is up for grabs in 2028, opposition to an unpopular president will not be enough.

If Democrats do not want socialists to define their party, they must define it themselves.

Thir agenda should combine secure borders with an earned pathway to citizenship, fiscal responsibility with targeted investments and practical solutions for the affordability crisis, support for allies like Israel alongside responsible diplomacy, improving public safety and a commitment to capitalism that expands opportunities to lift more Americans up and rewards hard work and innovation.

These positions should not be divisive, and reflect the kind of pragmatic, center-left agenda that can appeal to both the Democratic base and to independent, swing voters who decide elections in battleground states.

Ultimately, even if Republicans missed a chance to score political points or exacerbate Democrats’ ideological battle, this still highlighted a genuine Democratic vulnerability. Moderate and center-left Democrats should use this moment to not just oppose Trump, but to define the party around economic growth, affordability, public safety, secure borders, and effective government.

If Democrats want to win when Trump is no longer the villain, they must offer a forward-looking and inclusive agenda that shows Americans how Democratic leadership would improve their lives.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die. ”
