articles.title: Nathan Fielder reveals surprise documentary on Elizabeth Holmes
articles.summary: Comedian and satirist Nathan Fielder is preparing to publish a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, the former business executive convicted of defrauding investors in connection with health technology company Theranos. A trailer for the film, titled “You Can See Everything,” shows Holmes and Fielder seated close to one another locked in eye contact as she tells…
articles.body:
Comedian and satirist Nathan Fielder is preparing to publish a documentary on Elizabeth Holmes, the former business executive convicted of defrauding investors in connection with health technology company Theranos.

A trailer for the film , titled “You Can See Everything,” shows Holmes and Fielder seated close to one another locked in eye contact as she tells him she is not trying to “deceive” him.

The comedian briefly breaks character and asks her, “you’re being real right now?” to which she smiles and replies “I’m always being real.”

The film debuted over the weekend during a surprise screening at the Telluride Film Festival, after which Fielder took questions from the audience, The New York Times reported .

“I don’t know why I’m there,” Fielder said during a Q&A after the screening, according to the Times.

“I’m really struggling to this day to understand what I experienced,” he continued, according to the Times. “I’m excited for this movie to come out and for people to help me with what I experienced.”

Holmes is currently serving time in federal prison for a scheme to defraud investors in the blood-testing company Theranos. She invited Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim into her rented home in Southern California just weeks before she reported to prison in 2023.

The film, which was produced in conjunction with A24, is reportedly three hours long and slated to hit theaters on Oct. 16.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy attorney asks Trump for pardon after mistrial
articles.summary: Following the mistrial, prosecutors have the option of retrying the case, making a plea deal or dropping the charges.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Lindsay Clancy ‘s attorney said in a recent interview that he hopes President Trump will consider a pardon for his client.

A judge declared a mistrial last week after jurors failed to reach an agreement in the case.

In an interview with Good Morning America , attorney Kevin Reddington said he hopes an agreement can be reached between prosecutors and the defense and that Trump could consider a pardon.

Clancy is charged with murder in the deaths of her three young children. Prosecutors say it was a premeditated crime, while the defense says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and is not criminally responsible for her actions.

Prosecutors have yet to make a decision on whether they will retry the case.

Speaking to the press after the mistrial was declared, Reddington indicated the jury was moving to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, with one juror who was a holdout.

Following the mistrial, prosecutors have the option of retrying the case, making a plea deal or dropping the charges.

While Reddington suggested Trump could pardon his client, the president only has the authority to pardon those charged with federal crimes. Clancy is on trial in Massachusetts on state charges.

Trump briefly weighed in on the case last week, calling the deaths “a shame” and “a horrible tragedy.”

articles.title: Michigan rabbis press El-Sayed on Israel rhetoric
articles.summary: A petition signed by more than a dozen Michigan rabbis and Jewish leaders was launched Tuesday, pushing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to shift his rhetoric on Israel as lingering anxiety and frustration from the primary pour over into the general election over the progressive’s stance on the U.S. ally. “American Jews now feel forced to fight for the party they long claimed as their…
articles.body:
A petition signed by more than a dozen Michigan rabbis and Jewish leaders was launched Tuesday, pushing Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to shift his rhetoric on Israel as lingering anxiety and frustration from the primary pour over into the general election over the progressive’s stance on the U.S. ally.

“American Jews now feel forced to fight for the party they long claimed as their political home, asking its leaders to treat explosive bigotry and violence against our community as the national emergency it is not with platitudes, but with urgency and moral clarity,” said the petition, which was signed by 15 Michigan Jewish leaders, including Michigan Board of Rabbis president, Rabbi Aaron Starr.

The petition, which does not name El-Sayed but is clearly directed toward him, presses the Michigan Senate candidate to affirm Jewish safety, that Israel has a right to exist and to encourage the Jewish community’s civic and political participation.

“Treating Israel’s existence as a live question; using eliminationist language to describe Israel; raising an objection to ‘ethnostates’ that is never raised about any other state; or vilifying Israel as uniquely malevolent, are variations of the same demand: the dismantlement of only 1 out of the 193 countries in the world,” the petition said.

The petition refers to remarks El-Sayed made to The New York Times, which first reported on the petition , where he said he did not “believe in ethno-states, and I certainly don’t believe that our country is responsible to sustain ethno-states.”

“We reject cleverly worded arguments advanced to return the Jewish people to statelessness and powerlessness a position that a supermajority of Jews everywhere recognize as genocidal,” it added.

An El-Sayed campaign spokesperson declined to comment to the Times on the letter. The Hill has reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment.

The letter underscores the friction between Jewish leaders and El-Sayed, the latter of whom has been critical of Israel, has declined to say Israel has a right to exist, has called the events in Gaza a “genocide” and is against unconditional support to Israel.

Those positions are in stark contrast to his former primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who positioned herself as a staunch Israel ally while offering some criticism of Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

A super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, United Democracy Project, spent more than $30 million to support Stevens and oppose El-Sayed in the Democratic primary. El-Sayed narrowly beat Stevens, who has since endorsed him.

El-Sayed has sought to make inroads with the Michigan Jewish community since the fractious primary, including apologizing for saying “hurt people hurt people” in response to an attack against a West Bloomfield Township synagogue earlier this spring the FBI said “was motivated and inspired by Hizballah’s militant ideology.”

“I made a mistake,” El-Sayed said before the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus at the state party’s convention last month. “I should have issued a statement, of course condemning it, and it just should have been the full stop.”

“If my statement caused pain, I’m sorry,” he said. “That was not what I intended.”

El-Sayed faces a competitive battle against Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) in 2024. El-Sayed needs to shore up support among Black voters, Jewish voters and non-college-educated voting blocs — which made up a key portion of Stevens’s coalition in the primary.

The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report rates the Senate seat a “toss up.”

articles.title: Fetterman rejects ‘smears,’ ‘half-truths’ in Wall Street Journal report
articles.summary: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) dismissed what he called “smears” and “half-truths” in a recent Wall Street Journal piece, which reported allegations that he dodged constituents and ingratiated himself with conservative news outlets. “Per usual — lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous,” Fetterman said in a statement to CNN on Sunday, later adding, “No matter how…
articles.body:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) dismissed what he called “smears” and “half-truths” in a recent Wall Street Journal piece , which reported allegations that he dodged constituents and ingratiated himself with conservative news outlets.

“Per usual — lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous,” Fetterman said in a statement to CNN on Sunday, later adding, “No matter how many smears or stories, I’m proud to continue to deliver for Pennsylvania.”

The Pennsylvania Democrat –– who reportedly went almost a year without participating in a public event in his home state — also slammed text messages shared in the Journal report as being “stripped of any context and circumstances.”

The Hill has reached out to Fetterman’s office for comment.

Former staffers claimed to the outlet that the senator shows little interest in his job besides “cultivating relationships with conservative media figures and advocating for Israel,” according to the Journal.

One text exchange published in the report shows an aide telling him in September 2025 that officials at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) wanted to meet over worries about Medicaid cuts. Fetterman asked why he had to “keep meeting” with hospital officials, prompting the staffer to reply that it was about vaccinations and cuts to Medicaid, according to the report.

“Well I’m not,” the senator texted back. “I’m convinced they just want free trips to D.C.”

He apologized for the remark in his statement to CNN, calling it a “dumb joke” but added that he met with hospital officials in person and virtually.

“My office and I always have, and always will, advocate for CHOP, support their requests and any other needs that we can assist with,” Fetterman said.

Around that same time, the Journal reported the Democrat skipped the funeral for three police officers killed near his hometown of York, Pa. A staffer told Fetterman it would be a three-hour service, to which he replied that it “may be a nonstarter.”

He later told CNN he took steps to meet with the family members affected and share his condolences.

“On the day of that tragedy, we privately ordered flowers to be delivered for their families and expressed my condolences publicly,” Fetterman told the network. “In June of this year, I privately attended a Tunnel to Towers fundraiser in York for the families. I met with their chief and the family members directly to express my personal condolences.”

The newspaper’s report also suggested that Fetterman went on Fox News to discuss Israel and the Iran war after allegedly faking an illness to avoid meeting with disabled veterans. The Journal then noted the senator attended 26 of the 31 full hearings for his assigned committees in the past year, and that he did not speak in 20 of them.

Former Fetterman staffers have created an anonymous account on social platform X and have threatened to share more unflattering details about him, pointing to his frequent Fox News appearances and repeated support for Israel as he dismisses the rise of the left within his party.

The senator himself warned in July that he would leave the Democratic Party if it adopted an anti-Israel policy.

articles.title: Former Kennedy Center chair buys dismantled ‘Blue’ statue
articles.summary: The former Kennedy Center chair who was ousted by President Trump last year has purchased the “Blue” sculpture that was removed from the center’s grounds last week. David Rubenstein, the former long-term board chair who was fired by Trump and, alongside many of his colleagues, replaced with the president’s allies, bought the 24-foot aluminum sculpture…
articles.body:
The former Kennedy Center chair who was ousted by President Trump last year has purchased the “Blue” sculpture that was removed from the center’s grounds last week.

David Rubenstein, the former long-term board chair who was fired by Trump and, alongside many of his colleagues, replaced with the president’s allies, bought the 24-foot aluminum sculpture for more than $2 million, according to The New York Times , which first reported the sale.

The towering sculpture will be displayed in the National Gallery of Art’s Sculpture Garden, where Rubenstein serves as chair of the board of trustees, according to The Washington Post , which also reported the buy. It was purchased from a foundation dedicated to the late artist who created the sculpture, Joel Shapiro.

“Blue,” which depicts an abstract human figure “poised in mid-kick,” had stood outside the Kennedy Center’s REACH expansion along its $250 million Video Wall, which opened in 2019.

The Kennedy Center ordered the sculpture’s removal last week without notice, prompting the National Park Service to temporarily close part of Rock Creek Parkway while crews dismantled the massive piece.

The center said at the time the Joel Shapiro and Ellen Phelan Foundation would determine where the sculpture would go next.

The sculpture was subsequently returned to the foundation, which is run by Shapiro’s daughter, Ivy Shapiro, before Rubenstein purchased it. It is not yet clear when the piece will be installed at the National Gallery.

Rubenstein, a billionaire philanthropist, helped fund the $250 million REACH expansion where “Blue” was displayed.

The sculpture’s removal came amid a series of changes at the Kennedy Center under its new leadership. The board voted to close the center’s main building for two years to undergo renovations, while efforts to add Trump’s name to the building remain tied up in court.

Shapiro, who died in 2025, described the sculpture as a “creation of possibility,” according to the center’s website . Once installed at the National Gallery, “Blue” will join another Shapiro sculpture, his 1998 “Untitled,” already on display in the Sculpture Garden.

articles.title: How voters can overcome election sabotage: show up and vote early
articles.summary: Given the uncertainty of mail-in ballots, we need to encourage early in-person voting.
articles.body:
It is a sobering reality that in 2026, our own federal government is trying to keep millions of eligible Americans from voting.

Nearly every week, we see new evidence of the extraordinary steps the Trump administration will take to prevent voters from being able to choose their representatives. Last week’s explosive whistleblower report revealed U.S. Postal Service planning that could derail the midterms and reject tens of thousands of ballots. The Department of Homeland Security is launching criminal voter fraud investigations in nine states, several involving competitive congressional races.

Resources that could be going toward preventing human trafficking or domestic terrorism are instead going toward a phantom problem: vanishingly rare non-citizen voting. This follows an FBI raid of a voting rights group in Ohio and the intimidation of colleges and universities that use federal funds to support nonpartisan civic activities to help students vote.

Many scholars of global history note that such repressive actions follow the authoritarian playbook. For authoritarians, elections aren’t a healthy competition of ideas and candidates, and voting rights aren’t constitutionally protected rights that our ancestors marched and fought hard to expand. They are merely inconvenient barriers that prevent the consolidation of power. To control the outcome of elections, authoritarians specifically target the historically marginalized and groups that resist their agenda.

We cannot accept this. Every American from every state, every position and every political party — especially leaders who have taken an oath to protect our rights and serve the people — must unite to protect the right for everyone to vote and ensure the will of the people prevails. Every eligible voter must have an equal say in the decisions that impact our lives.

Holding free and democratic elections in America is not controversial nor partisan. Conservatives rely on the Postal Service to submit absentee ballots just like liberals and independents. The Republican governor of Wyoming, Mark Gordon, recently expressed concern about “ aggressive ” Justice Department officials examining voting machines in Cheyenne.

“I feel very strongly about the federal government coming in and taking our guns. I don’t like that,” said Gordon. “And I don’t like the federal government coming in and taking our votes, either.”

In the coming months, voting rights groups predict we will see more election threats. As organizers at Protect Democracy warn, “This year, every lever of federal power is being marshalled toward undermining a free and fair election.”

Rather than get discouraged or spread fear, we need to stay calm and carry on with even more vigor and resolve. The solution to massive voter suppression is massive voter mobilization. Given the uncertainty of mail-in ballots, we need to encourage early in-person voting.

In nearly every state and the District of Columbia, some form of early voting is available. Shout outs to Minnesota and South Dakota for being first out of the gate, allowing their voters to cast ballots as early as Sept. 18. Voting early is often faster and more convenient, and it reduces wait times for those who vote on Election Day.

Secondly, we can emulate the community spirit and organizing that successfully countered Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minnesota and across the country, this time to coordinate carpools to the polls, host voting rights trainings and organize creative and joyful voter awareness events.

In addition, we can inoculate against disinformation by sharing accurate facts about voting and the security of our elections. For example, it’s never been more important for democracy defenders to show up at places like county commission board meetings, where election logistics are handled, to counter conspiracy theorists spewing nonsense.

Finally, given that elections are run by states and local government officials, we can hold them accountable, demanding they do everything they can to keep polling sites open longer, make the voting process accessible and pledge to honor election results.

Research shows that the more voters hear about attempts at election interference, the more determined they become to show up to vote. Pairing awareness of the anti-voter agenda with empowering messages of what we can do to resist and overcome it works best. We need to honestly confront the challenges without catastrophizing them in a way that makes a dark future feel inevitable.

Nothing is inevitable. History has yet to be written. What happens next is up to us.

In a democracy, voters get to choose their leaders, not the other way around. As we face relentless attempts to interfere in the midterm elections, “We the People” need to be even more relentless to make our votes count.

Na Eng is chief creative officer at People For the American Way and author of “The Art of Saving Democracy: An Action Kit for Making Change. “

articles.title: GOP senator defends Bombardier after Trump threat
articles.summary: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) is defending private jet maker Bombardier from growing pressure from President Trump, who on Monday declared the Canadian aerospace company would no longer be able to sell planes in the United States. Moran, the senior Republican senator from Kansas, pointed out that Bombardier is a major employer in his home state,…
articles.body:
Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) is defending private jet maker Bombardier from growing pressure from President Trump, who on Monday declared the Canadian aerospace company would no longer be able to sell planes in the United States.

Moran, the senior Republican senator from Kansas, pointed out that Bombardier is a major employer in his home state, which currently features a competitive Senate race between Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton.

“This afternoon, I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain. I will continue working to see that Bombardier’s manufacturing operations not only remain in Kansas but continue to grow and create American jobs,” Moran posted on X, the social media platform, on Sunday.

Moran said Bombardier’s presence in Wichita supports a local workforce “of more than a thousand employees.”

“Kansas is home to a hardworking, skilled workforce, and I will continue welcoming leaders in aircraft and defense manufacturing to do business here in the Air Capital of the World,” he wrote.

Despite Moran’s defense, Trump on Monday declared that the U.S. market would be closed to Bombardier because he said Gulfstream, a subsidiary of General Dynamics, an American industrial and technology company, is blocked from doing business in Canada.

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough! Over 50% of their revenue comes from the United States — They live off American Buyers, American Companies, American Airports, and American Service — All while Canada blocks our GREAT American Banks, and Companies, throughout the U.S.A.,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

“They even blocked Gulfstream Aerospace from doing business in Canada — Completely unjust and unfair!” Trump wrote.

Bombardier said in a statement Monday that its manufacturing operations create “tens of thousands of US jobs” through what it called an “American footprint.”

“Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its US employees,” the company said. “Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country.”

The Canadian company’s supply chain includes more than 2,800 companies across the United States.

Trump’s threat to ban Bombardier from selling jets in the United States comes amid an escalating trade battle that has prompted strong pushback from Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $27.6 billion in American products took effect Tuesday. That followed the Trump administration’s 50 percent tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian imports taking effect last month, and Trump’s threats to tariff imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel starting next year.

articles.title: The Christian nationalism takeover of Congress
articles.summary: In his new bestseller “No Prophets,” Representative Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) argues that Christian nationalism poses a severe threat to American democracy and has established a “shadow theocracy” within the House of Representatives under Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.).
articles.body:
It’s not unusual for a member of Congress to write a book. Many have, and most of them are of little interest. I know, after reading too many of them.

What is unusual is for a member of Congress to write a book that makes the New York Times Bestseller list. But that’s the case with “ No Prophets .” The new book by Jared Huffman (D-Calif.) debuted in the Times this week as No. 6 of all best-selling hardcovers. No book could be more powerful or more timely.

“No Prophets” not only exposes how Christian nationalism is a serious threat to our democracy, it also reveals how, under the leadership of Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), Christian nationalists have, in effect, taken over control of the House of Representatives.

Huffman is quick to point out that Christian nationalism is far different from the old Moral Majority of Jerry Falwell. By mobilizing evangelical voters, Falwell worked within the democratic system to promote what he called “pro-life, pro-traditional family” policies. Today’s Christian nationalists are not out to improve democracy — they’re out to destroy it. Their stated goals are to establish the United States as a Christian nation, make Christianity the official state religion, tear down the wall of separation of church and state, and make the Bible, not the Constitution, our fundamental national document in order to achieve what Johnson calls “ biblically-sanctioned government .”

Christian nationalism is, according to Huffman, “America’s most dangerous political movement.” And what’s stunning is the extent to which it has already infiltrated the Congress. As Huffman describes the scene, “The Capitol complex teems with Christian nationalist power players, faith leaders, religious networks, advocacy groups, and a steady wave of religious programs converging with a common purpose: to embed right-wing Christian influence in government and manifest biblical dogma into policy.” It’s what he calls a “shadow theocracy” inside the Capitol.

The signs are everywhere: The Christian nationalist “ Appeal to Heaven” flag displayed in front of many congressional offices; ministers that roam the corridors and drop in regularly to pray with members; daily prayer breakfasts for Christians only; lobbyists who intercept members and hand them invitations to the next Bible study. All under the direction of Johnson, who reopened a tiny prayer chapel near his office where he told reporters he goes to “ seek the Lord’s guidance for what we do each day ” and who, in his first TV interview as Speaker, told Fox News host Sean Hannity : “Well, go pick up a Bible off your shelf and read it. That’s my worldview.” One would only wish he’d also read the Constitution.

The most important contribution of Huffman’s book is making the connection between Christian nationalism and Jan. 6. The attack on the Capitol was not just a political rally, Huffman argues — it was a fundamentalist religious revival. Christian nationalists were among its key organizers. Christian nationalists were bussed to Washington and led the march on the Capitol. Before invading the Capitol, many blew the shofar, carried huge wooden crosses, openly prayed with their hands aloft, and waved the “Appeal to Heaven” flag. One Capitol Hill police officer testified about being confronted with rioters carrying a sign reading “Jesus is my Savior, Trump is my president.” One year later, the Smithsonian labeled its online exhibit of photos and videos of Jan. 6 “Uncivil Religion.”

There is no doubt Christian nationalism was a driving force behind the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol. The Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the United States Capitol even appointed a special task force to examine the role of religion on Jan. 6. As Committee Chairman Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.) admitted to Huffman, they found that “right-wing Christian extremists actually had a lot to do with it.” And yet, the committee’s final 845-page report makes no mention of anything related to religion or Christian nationalism. Why? As Huffman reveals for the first time, Select Committee Vice-Chair Liz Cheney (R-Wyo.), for whatever reason, vetoed it. So one opportunity to expose the dark, violent side of Christian nationalism was lost forever.

Fortunately, there is some pushback. In 2018, Huffman and Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) launched the “Freethought Caucus,” a group of lawmakers dedicated to defending church-state separation. It started out with a handful of members, but today its ranks have swelled to 33 members — more than the Republicans’ Freedom Caucus.

Huffman describes the mission of the Freethought Caucus as “defending religious freedom, resisting theocracy, and advancing our nation’s core values, including civil rights, pluralism, rule of law, academic freedom, and the defense of science.” With those all-American goals, every representative should be a member.

Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito is embroiled in a second flag controversy, this time over the “Appeal to Heaven” flag, a banner that in recent years has come to symbolize Christian nationalism and the false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. articles.title: Trump posthumously awards Medal of Freedom to 9/11's 'man in red bandana'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump awards the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously to Welles Crowther, the heroic "man in the red bandana" who saved up to 18 lives during the September 11 attacks.
articles.body: President Donald Trump honored deceased volunteer firefighter Welles Crowther – also known as the "man in the red bandana" – with the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday. Speaking during Tunnel to Towers' "Steel Across America" event in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, President Donald Trump praised Crowther, whose actions during 9/11 saved up to 18 people's lives, sparking nationwide admiration and a series of documentary features on his bravery. "Today we also remember another hero of 9/11. After the plane hit the south tower, a group of people on the 78th floor were trapped with broken bones, charred skin and eyes and lungs filled with black smoke. Death was all about them. It was certain they were sure they were going to die. Then suddenly a rescuer appeared. They call him the man in the red bandana. Have you heard that term? The man in the red bandana has become more famous than me. I don't like it. Very unhappy. But he's become much more famous than me," Trump joked. "He's the man in the red bandana. He had found the only stairwell that barely survived. The stairwells were all knocked down. You couldn't get by. Impassable. He found an opening in one of the stairwells, and the impact was so great there was no other way down but this one little opening, this one little hole. And [he] traveled down from the 104th floor to look for those trapped and dying," Trump continued. "When he heard cries for help on the 78th floor, he began extinguishing the fires, blocking the exit, directing survivors who could walk, of which there weren't that many. He helped them out physically. They literally pulled him out toward the only working stairwell and carried those who couldn't walk. And he just did things that people said were not even imaginable because they knew they were dead. They said, 'we're goners.' One guy was screaming, 'we're goners! We're goners!' He didn't know those he helped and, nor who would have known, but he willingly made all of these trips up and down, up and down, up and down, over and over again, saving life after life," Trump added. "That rescuer was a 24-year-old equities trader and volunteer firefighter from Rockland County named Welles Crowther. And Welles' father, also a firefighter, great firefighter, had given him that bandana as a very special tribute when he was a boy. He probably knew something about his son. When asked why he always kept it, Welles replied 'with this red bandana, I'm going to change the world. I'm going to change the world with this bandana.' Little did he know, on September 11th Welles saved many, many people before losing his own life in the South Tower lobby. When the building came down, he was in the lobby and that building came down, thousands of tons of steel," Trump said. "Today, in honor of his incredible bravery and all of the other countless unknown acts of heroism that day, it is my privilege to award the very special, the highest honor that we give, the highest civilian honor, the Presidential Medal of Freedom. We want to award that to Welles and the Welles family. Welles is up there looking down at his mom and his sister, his family," Trump said. Trump was speaking during the Tunnel to Towers' "Steel Across America" event, in which the organization takes a 16,900 lb steel beam that came from the World Trade Center's South Tower across the country. The president also invited Crowther's mother on stage to speak about her son after revealing he had promised her years earlier to award the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honor, to her son. "That Welles' light still shines brilliantly today, even after 25 years, is testament to his legacy of courage, compassion and love for humanity that continues to inspire and uplift others," Alison Crowther said. "Wells, however, would not have been able to do what he did as effectively on 9/11 if it had not been for the training and experience he gained as a member of Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number one of Upper Nyack. Empire is a volunteer company and the members are fully trained firefighters. They have other jobs and responsibilities, businesses to run and their own families. But when the alarm goes off at any time, day or night, they respond to the call to save life and property. This is a calling. And Welles – following in the footsteps of his father, Jefferson – joined Empire at the age of 16. He was no longer an equities trader on 9/11, he was a firefighter," she said.

articles.body:
Former Republican Rep. Charlie Dent (Pa.) on Monday called President Trump’s social media posts referring to New Mexico as “New America” “bizarre” and accused him of “hurting his own team” ahead of the midterms.

MS NOW’s Peter Alexander asked Dent on “State of Play” about the president’s latest posts , including an AI-generated map with the “New America” label on the Land of Enchantment. The former lawmaker branded the posts as a “total distraction” from “real issues.”

“I mean, all these sorts of things that are completely irrelevant to Americans’ lives and, frankly, they think it’s bizarre, just renaming states and lakes and the Gulf,” the Pennsylvania Republican continued, referring to the Gulf of Mexico. “So again, a distraction, but these are not helping the president or his party.”

He added, “It’s hurting his own team. It’s almost like there’s an intentional act to undermine your own party’s prospects in the midterms.”

Dent said Americans likely see the president’s actions and think, “What is he doing?”

He urged Trump to train his focus on the cost of living and ending the Iran war but noted that the president “continues to obsess over the ballroom and the Kennedy Center and the Reflecting Pool.”

Trump signed an executive order late last month to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” amid his trade war with Canada, with Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on $27.6 billion in American products starting to take effect . Days later, a viral hoax claimed he signed an executive order on Sept. 1 changing New Mexico’s name to “New America.”

Fact-checkers like Snopes disproved the claim, noting that it came from a satirical social media account, but Trump appeared to be aware of the post and reshared it –– a map of New Mexico with “Mexico” crossed out and replaced with “America” –– on his Truth Social and the White House’s official social media accounts.

The president wrote later Sunday evening , “Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA. So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!!”

New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) said the issue was not “up for debate” and accused Trump of distracting Americans from the Iran war and high gas prices.

“While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work,” she wrote on the social platform X.

These incidents are not without precedent, as the president signed an order last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America.” It drew the ire of Mexican lawmakers and prompted their government to sue Google after the company displayed the Gulf as “Gulf of America” on its map for U.S. users.

The tech giant later did the same with “Lake America,” leaving the name Lake Ontario intact for non-U.S. users.

articles.title: How the AfD's rise could reshape German politics
articles.summary: In this Quick Take, Ian Bremmer breaks down the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and what it could mean...
articles.body:
In this Quick Take, Ian Bremmer breaks down the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's historic win in the Saxony-Anhalt state election and what it could mean for the country's political future.

The far-right party, considered extremist in many German states, came in first with 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result. It is the first time since World War II that a far-right party has won a German state election outright. The center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the ruling party, came in at just 17.2%.

Ian explains the forces driving the AfD's surge: economic frustration, anger over immigration, and opposition to Germany's support for Ukraine. He also lays out the party's core positions, including ending Ukraine aid, lifting sanctions on Russia, leaving the EU, and rejecting what it views as ideologically driven policies from Berlin.

Though the AfD cannot form a government alone, Ian argues the longstanding firewall keeping other parties from working with them is likely to break. A weakened federal government and no national election until 2029 could give the AfD the runway to grow even larger.

articles.body:
Republican strategist Doug Heye slammed President Trump on Monday for not directing more funding from his super PAC to a variety of GOP campaigns as the Republican Party fights to maintain its control of Congress this fall.

Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee (RNC), told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that the GOP’s prospects in the midterm elections are “bleak” due in part to a lack of campaign funding.

“Donald wants to spend money on himself. He doesn’t want to give things away, and he wants Republicans to earn it,” he continued, likening competition for campaign funding to Trump’s former reality TV show, “The Apprentice.”

The Atlantic recently reported that the president rejected urges from GOP strategists and leaders to expend more money from his super PAC, MAGA Inc. , on campaigns and chose instead to focus on funding TV commercials that boost his own image.

The president and other Republican leaders are scheduled to attend the RNC’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas this week. The two-day event, which kicks off Wednesday, seeks to drum up excitement among GOP voters ahead of the November elections.

“We’ll see how some of that, if any of that, changes ultimately in Dallas this week,” Heye said.

“But the other issue is then what Donald Trump talks about. … He tells voters we’ve never been hotter or richer, and voters don’t feel hot right now,” he added.

The strategist also pointed to the president’s sinking approval numbers , which remained at 33 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos survey released at the end of August. Heye explained that when he worked at the RNC, Republicans’ “magic number” for former President Obama was 46 to determine whether or not they could retake power in the House.

“Donald Trump is nowhere near that now,” he continued. “The maps are completely different now with redistricting by Democrats and Republicans, so you don’t have a 63-seat pickup opportunity, but Republicans know that their back is against the wall.”

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a nonpartisan election analyst, forecasts that Democrats have a 68 percent chance of retaking control of the House this fall. The parties are more evenly tied in the fight for the Senate, in which DDHQ finds there is a 50/50 split in the probability that each wins a majority of the upper chamber’s seats.

articles.title: Newsom admits democratic socialist ideas ‘mainstream’ in Democrat party: ‘Pretty aligned’
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the DSA on Medicare for all, climate change and fossil fuels.
articles.body: In an interview discussing his rumored 2028 presidential run, California Gov. Gavin Newsom asserted that the Democratic party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), especially when it comes to universal healthcare, climate change and moving away from fossil fuel usage. During an interview with PBS NewsHour, Newsom was questioned on what recent democratic socialist victories across the country mean for the Democratic Party. "If you have these candidates and this platform that is clearly animating the base, energizing turnout, should more of those ideas be worked into the broader Democratic platform?" Newsom was asked. "I think they are," Newsom shot back. "I mean, we want money out of politics, I’ve been supporting clean money campaigns for decades." NEWSOM TELLS DEMOCRATS TO BE IN THE 'ADDITION NOT SUBTRACTION' BUSINESS WITH SOCIALISTS The interviewer pressed Newsom further, saying, "There seems to be some distance between [Democratic] leadership and those DSA candidates." "But, not the ideas," Newsom responded. "I believe in universal healthcare, and I believe in Medicare for all, the party does overwhelmingly," he said. "And so, if it’s about more money in your pocket, lowering costs, getting money out of politics, if it’s about Medicare for all, I think we’re pretty aligned." He added, "It’s about recognizing that we’ve got a planet that is getting hotter and drier and that we’ve got to address the issue of climate change, we want energy security and we want to move off fossil fuels, that’s a DSA position, that’s a mainstream position within the Democratic Party." Newsom dismissed worry about democratic socialist influence in American politics, saying, "I think in many ways, it’s just a label … it’s just such a familiar label to me, we call them progressives." NEWSOM HIT WITH LAWSUIT THREAT AS WHISTLEBLOWER BEGS TRUMP FOR HELP WITH ‘MONUMENTAL’ FRAUD SCANDAL "Maybe it's just because I’m from California and I think it’s healthy … I’m not consumed by this," the governor continued, adding that the DSA’s ideas reflect "aspects and component parts of our party that we’ve always had and it’s a healthy dialectic within the party." Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom’s office for additional comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the DSA and to the Democratic National Committee for comment. The DSA is the pre-eminent socialist political group in the U.S. This year, the group rolled out an updated platform that includes eliminating the Senate and replacing the president and the Supreme Court with an executive and judiciary chosen by Congress. Additionally, the updated platform includes amnesty for all immigrants and defunding the Department of War. JENNIFER SIEBEL NEWSOM DODGES QUESTION ON HUSBAND GAVIN'S PRESIDENTIAL ASPIRATIONS This is in addition to the DSA’s already existing policy platform, which calls for an "immediate end to all deportations," free migration between countries without restrictive immigration controls, and "extending full voting rights to people with criminal convictions and noncitizens." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Once considered a fringe movement on the Democratic Party’s progressive wing, the DSA has been gaining relevance, with several of its members toppling longtime establishment party figures. This has prompted many to speculate that the DSA represents the Democratic Party’s future.

articles.title: Iran-backed attacks threaten a second major oil chokepoint as new risk emerges for US consumers
articles.summary: Houthi missiles and drones struck Aramco facilities across Saudi Arabia, threatening to squeeze both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.
articles.body: Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck Saudi Arabia with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones Tuesday, hitting multiple energy targets, including the facilities of the world's largest oil company. The attacks on Aramco, the state-owned national oil company of Saudi Arabia that produces 10 million barrels of oil per day, threaten to tighten pressure on a second critical oil route as the Middle East war continues to restrict shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Aramco notably supplies roughly 10% of the world's total oil demand. And attacks on its facilities raise the risk of higher oil, shipping and transportation costs that could hit U.S. consumers in coming months — just in time for the 2026 midterm elections. IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT? The attacks hit the southern Saudi Arabian cities of Jazan, Najran, Abha and Khamis Mushait, wounding 73 people and sparking fires at energy facilities and utilities that temporarily forced some operations to stop, according to Saudi officials. The Jazan site includes a refinery capable of processing roughly 400,000 barrels of crude per day, according to the Associated Press. Tuesday's strikes land at a particularly vulnerable moment for global energy markets. With oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz sharply reduced, Saudi Arabia has redirected more crude toward the Red Sea — increasing the importance of the Bab el-Mandeb, where the Houthis have already threatened and attacked Saudi-linked shipping. The Energy Information Administration estimates that just 4.9 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids moved through Hormuz per day in the second quarter of 2026, down from 21.6 million barrels per day before the conflict. Before the conflict 20% of the world's oil moved through the consequential waterway. Traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb, meanwhile, averaged 8.1 million barrels per day during the quarter as Saudi Arabia redirected more crude to bypass Hormuz amid ongoing conflict. That creates a potentially costly vulnerability: renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure or commercial vessels could put pressure on two crucial oil routes at once, raising the risk of higher crude, shipping and transportation costs that could eventually reach U.S. consumers. Brent crude was trading near $99 per barrel Tuesday. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Tuesday’s strikes, saying the group had used "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" against Aramco facilities, the Jazan industrial zone and a Saudi air base, according to Xinhua. RUBIO ACCUSES IRAN OF FLYING IRGC PERSONNEL INTO YEMEN AS HOUTHI THREAT ESCALATES The Houthis said the operation was retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen and threatened "stronger and wider strikes" if Riyadh’s military campaign continues. The escalation also comes with a warning already issued by President Donald Trump. After the Houthis struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea in July, Trump said the U.S. would hold Iran responsible if the group attacked ships again and threatened "major military punishment" against both Tehran and the Houthis. "If they do this again, the U.S. will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves," Trump wrote on Truth Social at the time. The warning followed the Houthis’ announcement of a maritime blockade targeting Saudi Arabia and attacks on Saudi tankers in the Red Sea. The escalation sent Brent crude above $100 per barrel amid fears that disruption could spread from the Strait of Hormuz to the Bab el-Mandeb. The latest strikes targeted Saudi territory and energy infrastructure rather than ships, leaving unclear whether the White House considers them to cross the line Trump drew in July. It creates a new test for the administration as Houthi attacks increasingly intersect with the wider conflict over Iran and regional energy supplies. The Trump administration has previously authorized U.S. strikes against Houthi weapons and infrastructure in Yemen in response to attacks and threats against American forces and shipping. A White House report says Trump directed those actions to defend U.S. forces and protect American national-security interests. The U.S. Maritime Administration also maintains an active advisory warning that the Houthis continue to pose a threat to commercial vessels in the southern Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb and the Gulf of Aden. From November 2023 through October 2025, the Houthis carried out more than 100 attacks on commercial vessels affecting more than 60 nations, according to the MARAD advisory. The attacks forced major shipping companies to avoid the Red Sea and reroute vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, adding time to voyages and increasing fuel, freight and insurance costs. The Houthis renewed that threat in July when they targeted Saudi oil tankers and threatened a blockade of Saudi shipping through the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia’s increased reliance on the route makes another sustained disruption potentially more consequential. The EIA says alternate routes used to bypass disrupted waterways are longer, more expensive and limited in capacity. The latest strikes threaten to revive pressure on the Red Sea route just as the Iran conflict has made the Persian Gulf route more difficult to use. The Houthis may lack the capability to permanently close the Bab el-Mandeb, but repeated missile, drone or tanker attacks could still reduce traffic through the waterway if shipping companies determine the risks are too high. Saudi Arabia condemned Tuesday’s strikes on civilian and economic assets and vowed to defend its territory. The Saudi-led coalition described the attacks as a "dangerous escalation" and said it would take measures to deter further attacks. The immediate economic impact will depend on how quickly Saudi Arabia restores affected operations and whether commercial shipping continues moving through the Bab el-Mandeb. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The next test could be whether the Houthis again target tankers or other commercial vessels. Another attack could put greater pressure on a waterway carrying an increased share of Middle Eastern oil — while also testing Trump’s warning that renewed Houthi attacks on shipping would bring U.S. retaliation against both the group and Iran.

articles.title: Reading scores near lowest point in 25 years
articles.summary: Reading scores in the United States were near their lowest point in 25 years, according to global exam results released Tuesday. American students were outperformed by students in Canada, Singapore and parts of China on the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) in reading — falling below the average score by over 30 points. The…
articles.body:
Reading scores in the United States were near their lowest point in 25 years, according to global exam results released Tuesday .

American students were outperformed by students in Canada, Singapore and parts of China on the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA) in reading — falling below the average score by over 30 points.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) evaluation measures how well 15-year-old students apply their knowledge to real-world problems. It is administered every three years to more than 80 countries, assessing mathematics, science and reading skills.

The scores released this year are the lowest average levels of performance observed in all three subject areas across all OECD countries, not just the U.S., since the test started in 2000.

The highest dropoff was in reading, with scores falling by 28 points across OECD countries between 2015 and 2025.

The World Population Review states that top-performing countries are often associated with “more equitable access to education,” whereas countries with lower PISA scores are linked to “higher levels of poverty and inequality that affect learning outcomes.”

Eight percent of students in the U.S. were top performers in mathematics, which is lower than the rate reported in parts of China, Singapore, Japan and South Korea.

U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon told The Hill that the scores “confirm a decade of stagnation and a devastating gap: we successfully propel our highest achievers, but the lowest-performing students are falling further behind — and have suffered a loss of learning in reading equivalent to nearly a year and a half of instruction compared to 2015.”

“This moment is a stress test for our nation’s future. To pass it, we must enact a hard reset that stops protecting a failed status quo and instead builds a system that empowers state leaders and embraces innovative learning options through school choice,” she said.

Early into President Trump’s term, the Education Department cut staff who were directly responsible for PISA’s administration, the New York Times reported, leading to participation rates in the U.S. falling below the minimum targets. OECD researchers warned that “ caution is required ” when interpreting the U.S. results because of this.

OECD Director of Education Skills Andreas Schleicher credited the score gaps between the U.S. and other Asian OECD countries to differences in attracting talent to the education sector.

“In the U.S. if you make a choice between a better teacher and a smaller class, you typically choose a smaller class,” he said. “In these countries, they save on the class size, but they get the best people to become teachers.”

He also reported that the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in classrooms differed in Western countries that use the technology to “make things easier for kids” as opposed to teachers in Asian countries using it “to make students think harder, work harder.”

articles.title: Appeals court upholds ruling barring IRS from sharing data with ICE
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld a lower court ruling blocking information sharing between the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after the immigration agency requested the last known address of millions of people. The three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit panel found…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Tuesday upheld a lower court ruling blocking information sharing between the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after the immigration agency requested the last known address of millions of people.

The three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit panel found ICE’s sweeping request for addresses of 1.28 million people who may be unlawfully present in the U.S. violated laws established in the wake of the Watergate scandal that bars the IRS from sharing information with other agencies unless it meets “stringent conditions.”

The ruling finds plaintiffs were likely to prevail in the matter and agreed the policy was reviewable under the Administrative Procedures Act, upholding a ruling from November of last year that blocked the IRS from aiding with deportations.

The IRS can share information with other agencies to help prosecute certain crimes, but those agencies must also list a specific point of contact.

“The IRS failed to require ICE to provide a ‘specific reason’ why the requested return information ‘is or may be relevant to [a qualifying] proceeding or investigation,’ as the statute demands,” Judge Cornelia Pillard, an Obama appointee, wrote for the panel.

“It entirely fails to ensure that ICE lists a federal employee, let alone one ‘personally and directly engaged’ in a qualifying investigation of a particular taxpayer. That failure has serious consequences. When ICE requested information on 1.28 million taxpayers in the summer of 2025, ICE identified the same person as the point of contact for every single request.”

The panel also found information sharing would violate privacy laws.

“The Data-Exchange Procedure reduces noncitizens’ privacy rights in their tax returns. By providing a distinct, automated pathway for ICE to request noncitizens’ information, the Data-Exchange Procedure deprives noncitizens of the protections that section 6103 guarantees to all taxpayers,” the panel found.

The ruling is another blow to ICE, which hoped to use the data to help locate migrants it is trying to support.

The Trump administration has pushed to link a number of government databases in the hopes of locating those who may not be lawfully present in the country.

articles.body:
It’s Tuesday, and it’s time to get back into the swing of things after a nice long Labor Day weekend (which is proving to be tough).

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Claire Leibowitz , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and cleibowitz@thehill.com.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. went into place at midnight Tuesday, impacting hundreds of American goods, including fish, cheese, apparel, carpets and metal products.

This comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney and Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told the U.S. that Canada would match U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” America’s neighbor kept its word, and also doubled its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent on Tuesday.

The Trump administration placed 50 percent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian products two weeks ago, goods such as hockey sticks, cement and wine. And it appears no negotiations are in the works.

Carney followed up on the retaliatory tariffs Tuesday, calling it a “shame” that Canada and the U.S. couldn’t reach a trade agreement.

“They wanted a say in our future agreements with other counties, and they were offering terms that would, over time, undermine some of the most industries in our country, including automobiles, steel, and forest products,” Carney said. “In short, they were asking far too much and offering far too little.”

Bombarding Bombardier : The president threatened Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier on Monday on Truth Social, saying it would no longer be able to sell products in the U.S.

Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) defended the Quebec-based jet and military aircraft company on the social platform X Monday because of its impact in Kansas.

“The presence of Bombardier in Wichita supports a local workforce of more than a thousand employees, who contribute their talent and expertise to our nation’s defense and aerospace capabilities,” Moran wrote.

“This afternoon, I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” he continued.

Bombardier made Wichita its U.S. headquarters in 2022 to expand flight tests and upgrade operations for its Learjet, Challenger and Global business jets.

Trump’s threats would not only impact Bombardier employees in Kansas, but also Texas, Arizona, Florida, Connecticut, Illinois, Delaware, California, Washington, D.C., and New Jersey.

“Bombardier aircraft are built with American-made components such as engines, avionics and many more key systems provided by great American companies,” the company said Monday.

“Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its U.S. employees. Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers and the communities in which we operate across the country,” it concluded.

North United States of America : President Trump raised tensions between the two countries even more on Monday by posting a map on Truth Social that showed an American flag draped over most of North America.

It also blanketed Iceland, Mexico, Greenland, islands in the Caribbean such as Cuba and Jamaica and part of Central America.

At a press conference Tuesday, Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called Trump’s post “absurd,” and said, “There is nothing funny or normal about making fun of the sovereignty of states.”

Republicans will flock to Dallas on Wednesday and Thursday alongside Trump for the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention.

The Associated Press has described the affair as “unusual.” Republicans have not held a midterm convention before, but Democrats did in the 1970s and 1980s.

Sticky situation: November’s midterms will prove difficult for both parties, as Decision Desk HQ has shifted its Senate prediction to “pure toss-up.” But it will prove particularly difficult for Republicans, who face a historical disadvantage as the party in power.

Record-high fuel prices amid the Iran war, trade tensions with Canada and Trump’s sagging approval rating could also dog the GOP at the polls.

The spectacle will aim to bolster Republican candidates and reflect on the president’s track record over the last two years to inspire voters to vote red all the way down the ballot on Election Day. Trump has even urged Republicans to “pretend” he’s on the ballot in November.

Taking attendance: Some candidates are avoiding the convention, though, as they fear associating their campaigns too closely with the president, The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports . Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) have decided to stay away and focus on campaigning in their respective states.

Trump plans to speak both nights. Other speakers include Vice President Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Attorney General Todd Blanche, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, Rep. Mike Johnson (R-La.), Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), RNC Chairman Joe Gruters , Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) and more.

The price tag is also bigger in Texas: The RNC is giving seats away, per The Independent, through a public lottery that would grant winners free tickets, front-row seats and VIP treatment. Otherwise, attendees must pay $25,000.

They can pay an extra $20,000 to be an “honorary delegate” and an additional $250,000 to get a donor seat at a roundtable with the president. On top of all of that, $88,600 could buy a commemorative photo. Seems like a lot more than the cost of that second bag of groceries.

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) is retiring, leaving her seat in limbo.

New blue: For the Democrats, Rep. Chris Pappas and scientist Karishma Manzur have faced a tightening race, according to recent polls.

Pappas has been endorsed by Shaheen and former Vice President Kamala Harris , while Manzur grabbed endorsements from Rep. Jamaal Brown (D-N.Y.) and other state lawmakers.

Manzur has also leveraged the fact that Pappas has been supported by American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), while Pappas has argued that his competitor has misconstrued how much he has received from the pro-Israel lobbying group.

Red race: For the Republicans, former Sens. John E. Sununu (N.H.) and Scott Brown (Mass.) have made their bids to return to Washington.

The former has been endorsed by members of Senate Republican leadership, including Sens. Tim Scott (S.C.) and John Barrasso (Wyo.) Polls show him comfortably leading Brown, who has been endorsed by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin , former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo and New Hampshire House Speaker Sherman Packard .

Shaheen’s seat leans Democrat, according to Cook Political Report.

Replacing Pappas: The race to replace Pappas in the 1st Congressional District between Stefany Shaheen (the daughter of Jeanne Shaheen) and Maura Sullivan has grown tense.

Shaheen has accused Sullivan of taking donations from AIPAC and Palantir. Sullivan has attacked Shaheen in ads and claimed she has a “fancy last name” and feels “entitled to your vote.”

Comedian Nathan Fielder shocked the film industry over the weekend, releasing a trailer for his documentary on former business executive Elizabeth Holmes .

The film, titled “ You Can See Everything ,” follows Holmes, who was convicted of defrauding investors while she was the CEO and founder of a blood-testing company called Theranos.

In 2018, Holmes and fellow executive Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani were charged with allegedly taking more than $700 million from investors while knowingly advertising false claims about her company’s technology. Holmes was found guilty on four of her 11 charges in January 2022.

Holmes invited Fielder and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim into her home 34 days before she was sent to federal prison for 11 years in 2023.

Not “ Dumb Starbucks ” anymore : Fielder’s popularity stems from his Comedy Central show “Nathan For You,” which focused on helping small businesses with out of this world ideas. In 2022, Fielder also released his own comedy on HBO titled “The Rehearsal.”

“You Can See Everything” is expected to be released on Oct. 16 and is being produced in conjunction with A24.
